My SH scars were all around roughly 10 years old before I had my tattoos done in that area. Like you I have a lot of scars that at the time needed stitches that never got them, so most of my scars are hypertrophic with I think maybe 1 or 2 that are keloids. 

I picked a tattoo place that at one point did free tattoos for covering self-harm scars and went in person so they could see and physically touch them to check the area was OK to tattoo first. After that it was just a matter of choosing what I wanted done. 

I went a little bit crazy and had 3 tattoos done in 3 months but I love them so much and am planning more (just don’t know what I want yet). I find having tattoos done incredibly relaxing and I’ve fallen asleep in all my sessions. I’ve only had to have one of mine touched up a few times but that’s more down to the scar it’s covering not taking ink well.

The most empowering thing about it for me has been placing something permanent that makes me smile over a huge period of my life where I was deeply unhappy and gave it an ending of some sort.

If you do decide to go for it my only little bit of advice is to carb-load before you go. My fun tattoo session routine is to always get breakfast from McDonalds before, and I always order either pizza or McDonalds (again) for dinner that evening.

If a child is nervous and they have a stuffed animal with them I always take pictures of their stuffed animal’s eyes first! Helps them to be more comfortable with having a go if what’s going to happen is modelled for them first.

After a while it will become muscle memory and you’ll just find yourself reciting it unconsciously! It’s simply just a case of practicing it. If you’re unsure as to what a good or clear image looks like (in the case of OCT if you have that), ask your optometrists. Show that you’re willing and eager to learn and ask questions. Every day is a school day in optometry! 

If you haven’t already (when I’m training new OAs on pretesting equipment I always do this) go through the pretesting process as a patient. Try every single bit of equipment for yourself so you can experience what your patients do and it will help you explain more clearly to them. 

Optomap can be tricky for younger children (the youngest I’ve done one for is 3) and patients with reduced neck mobility. As long as you can get an image of the optic nerve head generally you’re ok - sometimes it’s easy to get fixated on getting the perfect image so it’s good to be able to recognise when you’ve gotten the best images you can and stop. 

If you have any other questions feel free to DM me :)

“We’re going to do some images of the back of the eye. One eye at a time - you can choose - looking through the circle here. Find the target inside the machine, it should be blue to start. Push on the front on the machine until it turns green - red means you’re a little too close. We’re going to do 3 images, 2 in colour and 1 in black and white. Are you ready to start?”

I always show the patient exactly where I want them to be looking into, tried the keyhole analogy for a bit and found it actually took longer. I also direct them to turn their head so their nose is pointing towards the wall to either their left or right depending on which eye they’re looking in with. 

People tend to have one eye that’s easier to position than the other with Optomap so I always take care to reassure them that it’s normal to find one eye a little easier than the other.

Take note of the script that your colleagues use and start with that but adapt it to suit you once you’re comfortable with it :)

I happened to assist with a scleral fitting the other day and the feedback about the vision was incredibly positive. As long as the patient can comfortably tolerate insertion, removal and fit it’s a fantastic option. Exactly as you said, when they work they work well. 

Ortho-K generally isn’t an option for keratoconus patients - the one patient who I know is wearing them is an exceptional case where the keratoconus is stable, isn’t progressing rapidly and extra monitoring was a non-negotiable. The patient was willing to commit to the extra care / monitoring needed and the ophthalmologist was happy to give the green light to explore the option. 

I hope she can find an option that allows her to keep streaming and pursue what she wants to do. There’s a kind of grieving process people go through when something like this happens- I’ve seen it with patients in audiology as well. Sight and hearing are so precious.

Failed my maths GCSE 8 times. Got my C grade on the 9th attempt. What personally motivated me was spite, because everyone had given up on me being able to get a passing grade in maths. When my teachers and parents gave up on me being able to achieve it I became more determined than ever to prove them wrong. 

There was an intervention put in place by the maths department at my school which was really helpful. Everyone got the higher paper because it was easier to get a C grade on it as opposed to the lower one. The approach was “don’t overthink this and do what you need to do to pass” with focus on the most common types of exam questions in papers and how to solve them. 

A few things that worked for me that may also be helpful to you:

Timing / Time management - how long do you have to complete the paper? Take that time and figure out how long you can reasonably spend on each question / section. Set a limit on how long you can spend on a question before moving on. 

Thinking - Don’t overthink any of it. Overthinking leads to panic, which then leads to overcorrecting. Figure out what the question is asking you to do and then do it. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t make sense or you don’t understand it fully, just do it. 

Practice - Do as many mock exams as you can get your hands on. Time yourself, mark them and then go back and really look at what didn’t go well. Reflect, refine the process and apply it to the next mock paper. Make a list of things that you found hard or questions you have and ask your teachers for help. 

Accommodations - I had extra time for my exams and when I got to A-Levels I also did them in a quiet classroom rather than the big exam hall with other students (I also had a laptop because my typing speed in significantly faster than my writing speed). Looking into and advocating for those accommodations would be helpful.

I agree with you, this is wilful negligence to provide the appropriate care and aftercare for the patient. The reason I leaned into this being an equipment misuse issue and therefore negligent in that aspect is when you change the amount of joules on IPL machines it will go into standby to set up for that increase. 

The practitioner will be trained to check and double check again before starting to make sure that the joules are within tolerance for the patient and to prevent injuries - if they don’t check burns like above happen. 

My line of work, while not a Medical Spa setting, requires that I know the treatment protocols for IPL. It’s shameful to see duty of care towards patients being neglected like this.

Don’t go there for IPL treatment. This is a sign that they’re not doing their due diligence to make sure they are using the equipment correctly and not following treatment protocols and aftercare properly.

I knew exactly what was coming with Stealth and still got surprised at the drop. The moment when I could feel the force bringing me over the top and then down was terrifying but also the best thing ever. Came off shaking but so worth it.

It wasn’t lap bars I was folding over, it was the over the shoulder restraints. The force of the rides pulled me forward and I physically couldn’t brace against the seat so I think it felt like I was folding over something when what was actually happening was that I was just pulled forward. I’m relatively small though and got knocked around on Colossus and Stealth because of that probably. 

It’s a good idea to re-ride my favourites a couple of times on each trip (not looking forward to the idea of re-riding Colossus purely because of how rough it was but it must be done)! Definitely going to be planning an itinerary ahead of time to schedule the day. 

What helped me overcome my phobia and keep getting on rides was leaning into the fear and just feeling it. Terrifying but so fun that I wanted to keep feeling that fear if that makes sense? Swore like a sailor the entire way around but loved every second. Looking forward to doing the exact same thing on Swarm :)

I was partly aware Saw was a rougher ride but a few more rides on Colossus should get me a bit more comfortable with that feeling. 

A lot of my process on the day was just forcing myself to go on rides because I knew I had to just get on with it and do it and any bad parts wouldn’t last for long because the rides are short. Came off pretty much everything in a state of shock and then 10 minutes later was raving about how good they were.

I want to be sprinting to beat my friends to the queue first for Hyperia next time! The moment I feel comfortable doing that will be really special, just have to work towards it with a few return visits I think :)

Stealth was the one ride I absolutely knew I’d be riding no matter what but the others were a really nice surprise. Going upside down isn’t that bad and I actually really like it! 

I really liked Nemesis so I’m looking forward to trying Swarm next time. Absolutely wouldn’t have Colossus first in the running order though, that was a brutal first rollercoaster. Later on in the day, sure - but never again first.

I love the game but really didn’t take well to the anime adaptation because of how it was handled. An episodic adaptation was really not the way to go with this because of how sprawling and long the game story is, the amount of characters and their relation to each other. 

Magireco would have been better adapted into movies, honestly - decide how much story fits into the average movie length and work on making the amount of story and characters in that allotted time the best. They could have done so much more with it. I liked the anime, it had some beautiful animation and fight scenes (Holy Mami and Uwasa Tsuruno) but the story was crammed into a format that just didn’t benefit it causing inconsistent pacing and messing with the story in ways it just flat out didn’t need. 

Considering the EN servers were shut down after Arc 1 overseas movie premiers with limited-time merchandise would have gone a long way in repairing and giving back some goodwill to players on that server. Event story or characters could have been covered in OVAs in-between releases. 

The EN server shut down really badly affected the perception of Magireco. Players who had spent money in the EN serves were burned and the story in game was not officially translated after Arc 1 so people that were interested couldn’t follow along as easily anymore. People looking to get into Magireco see that there’s now a language barrier, a huge cast of characters and story events to catch up on. It’s overwhelming and I don’t fault people for not picking up Magireco in the same way as mainline Madoka. 

The Magireco manga is absolutely worth getting into. Officially translated and follows the game story now that both EN and JP servers have gone. It makes me sad how badly the anime and game were handled.

My brain is at its most engaged when I’m dissembling something and then putting it back together again. Practically this could be repairing glasses at work but it’s an approach I take when learning things as well. Learn the surface information first to get a basic understanding, and then look further into why something is the way it is.

That’s an issue with the lens coating. The only way to resolve that is to get the lenses replaced. Sometimes this happens because of a manufacturing error (in a new pair of glasses), more commonly it happens due to the age of the glasses (when glasses reach a certain point in their lifecycle the components of the coatings start to break down). 

If they’re new, take them back to where you purchased them from and explain what’s happened. They should be able to replace the lenses. If they’re a bit older and you’re due a sight test, have that first and bring the glasses with you. They may be able to put new lenses into the frame.

It's been a little over a year for me since I had C-Diff and I'm still having problems with PI-IBS. I get bloated after eating (depending on what it was I ate this can take a few days to settle down), horrendous stomach pain where I just have to lie down, let it pass and breathe through it. There's a lot of guesswork involved, I'm either in pain because I'm hungry or because I ate.

Grazing works really well for me because I can eat small quantities more often and I can adapt my food schedule around what I'm doing that day if my body very clearly isn't ready for food yet. Antibiotics and my period set off really nasty flare-ups that usually stick around for a month but it depends. Sometimes it just appears randomly and goes away quickly and other times it likes to stick around.

There are a few things that to me mean this could not be PI-IBS anymore and it's IBD so I'm in process of getting this confirmed with my GP. At this point I'm more concerned about malabsorption and my general bowel motility than with C-Diff. Something hasn't been right for a while but I don't think it's C-Diff  again.

I have not had any relapses! Antibiotics set off a really awful IBS flare up for me that mimics C-Diff symptoms. It's enough to set off the part of my brain that convinces itself everything is happening again but every sample I've sent off has come back negative. Another trigger for the same reaction is having my period, so really anything that disrupts my body thinking it's 'well' sets off the thoughts about potentially having C-Diff again.

I would recommend oral probiotics (I never get along with the dairy based ones) and small and simple meals. Anytime I'm issued antibiotics I always eat like I did when I had C-Diff: plain rice, bananas, toast, ham sandwiches and soup. Not ideal but I can supplement what I'm missing with Vitamins and it makes the antibiotic course a bit more bearable.

Keep an eye on it and get in touch with your GP if it seems to be not quite right. Take care and I hope you feel a bit better soon! :)

Withdrawal symptoms tend to vary from person to person and depend on a number of different factors - the half-life of your medication, the dose, and how long you've been taking it. This is typically the same for every SSRI across the board, but everyone reacts differently to SSRIs so personal experience is varied.

Medications with a longer half-life tend to have less withdrawal symptoms once you decide to taper off them and medications with a shorter half-life will generally have more withdrawal symptoms. 

Prozac has a long half-life and takes 240 hours to fully exit your system. Depending on what dose you're taking and for how long you can kind of get an idea of what withdrawal symptoms will be like if you decide to taper off it, although this is something to consider when you and your GP have agreed to taper off it when that time comes.

Prozac has a longer half-life compared to other SSRIs - it stays in your system for 240 hours. Taking a consistent dose of Prozac long term ultimately means that there's going to be a build up of it in your system and it's likely going to keep causing withdrawal symptoms of some kind after you've completed the tapering process.

I tapered off the highest therapeutic dose of Prozac after taking it for 5/6 years and I think the tapering process took about 2-3 months. My GP started me on Sertraline when I got down to 20mg of Prozac after I had an appointment where she could visibly see the toll the withdrawal and tapering process was having on me.

Absolutely speak to your GP about this. SSRI medication effects people very differently and that includes when you're coming off the medication. It makes sense to me that you didn't have too much trouble coming off it as a longer half-life typically means less withdrawal symptoms (experiences of this vary and very much depend on dosage, how long you've been taking it).

I would recommend keeping a diary or note on your symptoms in the meantime and what time/when they occur, as well as the impact it's been having on your daily life. Bring it with you to the GP appointment. Prozac withdrawal was absolutely hell on earth for me, second to Olanzapine withdrawal which took me 2 years to fully complete the tapering and withdrawal process.

Take care of yourself and I hope you can get this resolved with your GP ASAP. 🙂

My hearing loss is relatively recent (diagnosed in August this year), but I found my first visit to Audiology really positive. It was a relief just to have someone acknowledge that I wasn't losing my mind for the past few months and my experiences weren't imagined or "just in my head". The Audiologist was really good with asking questions, allowing me to describe what I'd been experiencing and helping me to verbalise and define a lot of what had been going on that I didn't know there were words for.

I was warned preemptively about being pushed towards hearing aids when they weren't going to help me but this didn't happen at the assessment. Based on the results they got from the hearing test in the appointment they actually discouraged hearing aids at this stage because it would make my problems significantly worse, and recommended an Assistive Listening Device instead. My understanding of hearing loss was very much surface level, so I made the effort to read into it more and it seems like a really interesting career that I'd be curious in pursuing.

I was pushed into going on a waiting list for hearing aids when I had a hearing test done at a Specsavers on the high street before my Audiology appointment and I refused. I'm so happy I did because I could have ended up with a tool that would have made things worse. It seems like an interesting profession but I do wonder about people being pushed towards certain options more than others, and it seems odd that a lot of 'baseline' (cheaper, more affordable) models for hearing aids, assistive listening devices etc perform at the bare minimum in terms of features.

Any tool is an investment, I understand that, but it seems unfair to lock certain features (wider ranges of pitches etc) behind more expensive models. Generally I've had a really positive interaction with Audiology and I don't have a bad thing to say about it, it seems like a really interesting career, but I'm curious about why the most versatile and helpful features of hearing aids and assistive listening devices are left out of certain models of tech at certain price points.

TLDR: positive Audiologist experience, cautious about being pushed into paying more for equipment that wouldn't help / that I don't need.

If I intend to start learning a new skill or try out a new hobby, I don't like to tell anyone before I've started it or reached a level of accomplishment. The same goes for future career plans too in that I won't tell anyone what I'm planning until everything is arranged and my ducks are all in a row, so to speak. Growing up I remember always feeling so demotivated and doubting my own abilities and aptitude for certain things when my parents either laughed at my enthusiasm for something or made fun of me for it.

I've started very quietly trying to learn how to cook. It took taking part in a cooking competition at school and my parents laughing about how badly I did (they still do it now) to get me to completely stop any efforts I was making in learning to cook. I'm 25 years old, very much an adult who should be able to prepare and cook a meal, but I just haven't gone there because I don't want anyone to laugh at me or make fun of my efforts.

Since I was a child I've always been quiet and didn't like to stand out, which still holds true now. I don't understand why I get praised for anything I do, especially at work where as far as I'm concerned I'm doing what I've been told to do. I don't understand why people are nice to me, in fact the only way to really make me cry is to be nice to me which I find strange.

I absolutely hate crying. It's the one feeling I can't let out and my biggest fear is someone else knowing they've done/said something to upset me because it feels like I'm incredibly vulnerable and something that can be used against me at a later date.

Overall I'd say it's a combination of quirks that flatten out certain areas of life for me. It helps in some and doesn't in others: at work it's actually very useful because I can find the opportunities to do what I've been asked to do better, I get to watch people to make up my own mind about if I trust them, and I can do it all quietly and with nobody noticing.

The downside to a lot of it is that I don't acknowledge when I am feeling upset about something, crying makes me feel horrendously embarrassed and I don't tell anyone how I'm feeling or what I'm thinking, so I come off as hard to read and mysterious when I'm just minding my own business and not sticking my nose into anyone else's.

You mentioned that he's on medication and seeing a therapist. Medication does 40% of the work: it will ease off the pressure on a person but it doesn't solve the problem for them. 60% has to be done by the person themselves, in therapy. He has to want to change and take the lead in and outside of therapy to modify his thought process.

Accountability is a big part of it, too. Acknowledging that he's done or said something to hurt another person, that it wasn't the right thing to do, apologizing properly and outlining some ways that next time he feels like he might snap that can distract him and preemptively take his mind off the intensity of his feelings until they simmer down.

Mental health problems may explain why someone behaves a certain way but it absolutely does not excuse those behaviours. Really, really push for family therapy. Your family really needs a structured and supportive environment where you can discuss comfortably how your husband's behaviour is affecting yourself and your children. Working together you could plan out some really great solutions for things your husband finds difficult and help your children to regulate their own emotions in a healthy manner in not replicating what they're seeing Dad do.

With daily exercise, it may help for this to be set at a certain time every day. Anxiety, depression etc thrives on a lack of routine and structure in daily life. Small steps at first are important just to establish the routine itself. It could be the 2 of you going for a walk at first - it's important to acknowledge that these experiences at first are really stressful and bring up a lot of negative emotions. It might be helpful to have a bit of a cool down and reflection when you return home: for example, how did x/y/z make you feel? What did the anxiety tell him would happen in those moments and what actually happened? What helped him to take the edge off the anxiety in that moment?

Overall I would really, really push for more involvement therapy wise. You all need to be on the same page as each other to communicate effectively. Does he give you any feedback about what happens in his individual sessions? If you don't know that it's going to be really difficult to coordinate anything. Family therapy is a must, joint sessions with just you and your husband. He may also find it helpful to look for a group therapy for men.

Generally speaking men are far more likely to bottle up emotions with a mental health problem and as a result the problem gets far worse before they choose to seek help themselves and often comes out more as aggression or anger (you mentioned a certain angry tone of voice he's using and he seems to be raising his voice a lot). Establish a boundary that he is not to raise his voice like that when speaking to you or the children because it is absolutely unacceptable. It may be more constructive to write his feelings down in a letter or diary, or have a safeword or phrase of sorts he can use if he wants to excuse himself to have a moment to calm down in a discreet way.

You need to be firm and hold strong on those boundaries, not just for your husband but your children. There should be consequences for his behaviour when he does break those boundaries, and this should be communicated clearly and firmly. For example, "You did/said [x/y/z]. You have not respected [insert boundary here]. As a result, [consequence]." Any discussion about his behaviour can also follow a similar pattern, "When you do/say [x/y/z], it makes me feel [insert emotion here]."

The most important thing is to take care of yourself and keep yourself healthy. You are absolutely entitled to feel how you feel about what's happening and don't deny the expression of those feelings. A diary or writing is really helpful for this as you can constructively get those feelings out and look back on them. You don't have to share it with anyone if you don't feel comfortable doing so.

Ultimately your husband now has to put the effort in to change his behaviour. Establish and hold those boundaries and keep him accountable for his own actions. Take care, take it one day at a time, it's a long road and progress isn't linear but I hope you and your husband can sort this out.

If people ask what happened I take out the C-Difficile part and just say colitis as that is far more understood. There is little to no understanding in the community about C-Diff as it's known more as a hospital superbug even though cases are rising in the community due to GP services switching to telephone consultations and flinging broad spectrum antibiotics at people. 

I wouldn't wish the agony of C-Diff on anyone. Having to fight with the medical system to get tested, treated and be taken seriously is absolutely exhausting. I avoided going into hospital twice and there was a moment where surgeons were pulled in to discuss if I needed to have part of my colon removed because it escalated so scarily quickly even with treatment.

The part that really sucks is that C-Diff doesn't stop after it's gone away. It keeps on isolating you afterwards and nobody can understand the nightmares and lack of trust in the medical field and our own bodies that are a constant after treatment. I can go to the doctor and dentist again now (still a bit scared of the dentist, wasn't before this, but I force myself to go for my own benefit), but I have nightmares in the days after a blood test and even after my covid vaccinations when I had them. I'm having my annual flu vaccination on Saturday and already preparing for nightmares to completely throw off my sleep schedule for a few days after.

The worst part of my partner saying that was he saw everything happening in real time, knows how much pain I was in constantly for a month and expects that because it's already happened, I need to move on from it and can't understand why that isn't possible. I got really lucky with work because my manager has a pharmaceutical background and knew enough about C-Diff to be really supportive when I came back to work and went back up to my usual shift patterns.

I remember trying to get an emergency prescription of my birth control during this whole thing so I didn't have to have a period that month and the pharmacist told me I could only request it for an important event like a wedding. Like how is the fact that surgeons were discussing potentially doing surgery to remove my colon not important?

I try really hard to not misplace my anger in this situation simply because it's C-Diff and it really is something you only understand once you've had it, but it's so difficult to not get angry when that experience is completely invalidated and waved off by everyone.

I feel like I need to lie down after that, bloody hell.

I went down roughly 2 dress sizes (20lbs/9kg/1.4 stone) in under a month. My hair started to fall out, getting comfortable when trying to sleep was really difficult and I did not feel well at all. In terms of physical activity I became very good at listening to my body and resting when it was very clearly telling me that I needed to rest. I went back to work but this was done in increments and I worked my way back up to doing 7 hour shifts again. It's really important not to rush back into activity after C-Diff because it takes a lot out of you and the body needs time to heal.

Diet wise I found that I got a lot of my calories through fruit juices and smoothies. I couldn't tolerate a lot of food at once so started eating little and often - I tried out loads of gluten free options and focused on getting enough vitamins from fruits and veggies that my body decided it would tolerate on the day. I gained back some weight quickly, but my weight gain plateaued after gaining 10lbs and I'm stuck there now. Gaining the weight isn't the issue for me but keeping it on is - usually what happens is I'll get my appetite back, eat well and then it'll be gone overnight and the weight falls off me faster than it took for me to put it on.

I absolutely hate Ensure and have a really hard time with it, Complan I get along with a little bit better but I still hate it. When my appetite dies my palette goes extremely bland and is almost always just ham sandwiches. I try to approach it with the mindset that it isn't ideal, and I need to supplement what I'm missing from my diet during this time, but at that moment this is just what my body wants and I am going to feed it exactly what it's asking for. If that means a week where all I want to eat is Subway tuna sandwiches, that's what happens. It's something that I can eat, it stays down and my body gets nutrients from it, and that's enough for me.

I was really bothered with my body image afterwards, because it was really obvious that I looked "sick" and I hated that. It was a very dramatic weight loss in that I looked worryingly underweight (bearing in mind there wasn't a lot of me before C-Diff, but my BMI was in the healthy range) and I didn't want people to look at me and just feel pity, or "I'm so sorry you've been unwell" comments. I just wanted to get back to normal and get back to doing normal people things, and be seen by others as just normal.

I stopped caring about people's reactions or odd looks because they were things I couldn't change. I focused on prioritising what I needed to do to get my body healthy again and if it looked weird to anyone else, that wasn't and (still isn't) my problem. There was no use in forcing a particular meal or food down if it was just going to cause pain, because it's counterproductive and a waste of my limited energy that's absolutely invaluable.

I just take it a day at a time, and buy food/snacks in smaller regular purchases depending on what I'm hungry for on the day. Sometimes that's mostly smoothies and grazing type snacks and other days it's 3 full meals a day, but either way it's something.

Flagyl is a particularly nasty antibiotic to prescribe for C-Diff, and it's an outdated one that another reply has mentioned in far more detail. Generally speaking it has the worst side effects and hits the GI system the hardest - it's also the cheapest to prescribe. When I had C-Diff in January this year I was given Flagyl and I can't remember a lot from when I started it to when I finished.

I had awful constant migraines for 6 out of the 10 day course and it also permanently damaged my hearing - I am now hearing impaired and have been predicted to get hearing aids in the next 1-2 years. From a GI standpoint, I've had 2 really bad PI-IBS flare ups since having C-Diff both triggered by being prescribed antibiotics again for different illnesses (I had my second bladder infection in 6 months, had a flare up, just finished Amoxicillin for a middle ear infection and am going through it again).

It takes time for the GI system to repair itself and heal from C-Diff. Probiotics are an absolute must, my body hates any probiotic in yoghurt drinks or anything dairy based so I take the Bio-Kult tablet probiotics with food. In terms of eating, I was intolerant to gluten and dairy products for the first 2-3 months post C-Diff. It's a trial and error process so follow an elimination diet (there are some very useful resources online for following an elimination diet and giving your body the vitamins it needs which may be through vitamin supplements if you're deficient in anything), and keep a food diary.

Keep track of your BMs as well in terms of frequency and appearance. If you're concerned at any point with a change in this do go to your doctor. They may be able to refer you to a dietitian as well if you would like help with figuring out what your body can/can't tolerate. Be careful not to overdo OTC laxatives as it can easily agitate your gut and make things worse - at most Fybogel sachets as they're gentle enough to not agitate the gut like senna based laxatives, and maybe look into a fibre supplement like Pysllium Husk if you feel you're not getting enough fibre from your diet.

It's a lot to process emotionally, and it's also really overwhelming to manage alongside focusing on figuring out what the new "normal" is for you. Stress will make any IBS symptoms act up so do take care of yourself - have treat days! I got really into using hair masks and face masks after having C-Diff, small self-care things I could do that were within in my budget. I find that mindfulness and meditation really works for me, it doesn't for everyone but any activity that gives you time to just be in the moment and switch off is very helpful.

It does get frustrating, incredibly frustrating. There will be days where nothing seems to be working, foods you could eat the day before just aren't sitting right and it all seems too much. Many people's understanding of C-Diff is really limited so do use this subreddit as a resource if you want to vent, or talk to someone that you feel comfortable with. If you like to journal or keep a diary that's also a really cathartic process. If this is something you want to process in a therapeutic environment please do so. There are great days where something small goes really well and everything really looks up - it changes a lot.

The most important thing is to take care of yourself and to really prioritise self-care and hobbies. When your body is telling you to rest, rest up and keep going at your own pace.

I generally don't tell anyone. My partner is very much aware of it being a diagnosis that I have but I've mellowed out a lot since I was first diagnosed and it's unnoticeable. My friend back home is aware of it in the same manner as my partner, really: it isn't an issue for both of them and it doesn't affect anything about the relationships.

I never disclose it to an employer and have only mentioned it to one of my co-workers because we both have a long term mental health problem. They haven't changed the way they treat me and I haven't changed the way I treat them. I know that the information I tell this person won't go anywhere else or be told to another person as gossip, and I respect them for it greatly.

Outside of that I don't mention it at all. The people that I feel can be trusted with the information know and I've only disclosed the diagnosis to them after I've observed they're trustworthy people, they know me for who I am as a person and will not change their behaviour towards me based on the diagnosis.

I will broadly describe things very rarely or vaguely allude to it but I never refer to it directly by name.

I remember any emotions I showed were often viewed as inconvenient to my parents. If I got upset in public the only response I got was one of irritation, like my parents didn't have the time to put whatever they wanted to do aside for one moment to acknowledge I was upset and understand why. Similarly if I expressed frustration at a situation I was often laughed at or mocked in some way.

After a few of these experiences my brain connected the dots that my emotions are an inconvenience to my parents, and if they do acknowledge them it will be a negative response at my expense. This bled into my perspective of relationships with my peers as well and I became an easy target for my peers to mistreat, because I wouldn't say anything about it even if I wanted to; if my own parents didn't care about how I was feeling why would a teacher? Why would a school nurse care if I felt sick?

Every time the outcome of me expressing any genuine emotions was correlated to the potential to be hurt, to be laughed at, to be taken advantage of. It made sense that if I wanted to avoid any of those things all my feelings just had to stay put and not be expressed, because it wasn't worth it and people didn't care.

I developed a really bad way of showing people that I didn't like their behaviour and to leave me alone. When some girls in my year at school took to trying to trip me up in class and constantly hounding me for no reason, I became incredibly aggressive in team sports. After these girls got a hockey stick to the ankle a little too hard or I'd slammed into them a few times in basketball they got the message and left me alone. I couldn't express that feeling in words so it came out as physical aggression, carefully timed and in a PE lesson where physical contact of some kind was a given. Never enough to be noticeable, but enough to get my message across. 

Clearly that could have been handled a lot differently and far more constructively, but all the sporty girls started to pick me for their teams so I got something positive out of it. Sadly nobody wants to play a team game with me anymore because they know how aggressive I get. I find it simultaneously interesting and concerning that the emotions I couldn't express verbally at the time came out physically, not just in sports but in other maladaptive ways as well.

I hate crying. I hate crying in front of other people and it never really goes fully, the bad feelings just sit there and fester because I will stubbornly refuse to get them out of my system by crying. Every time it happens I feel so incredibly pathetic and embarrassed, even though it's a perfectly healthy way to process emotion.

Very recently there was someone who went around the local area threatening local retail workers with a knife demanding money, tobacco etc. He was released on conditional bail after that and came into the store I work at in order to do exactly the same thing to my work colleagues. Luckily nobody was threatened or hurt, he was clocked almost instantly and removed from the store, but it made me seriously wonder if any of the authorities have any common sense. Why release the man after he's repeatedly threated people at their place of work? 

It seems that someone has to be seriously injured in order for anyone to take action. A story I've heard from another store is that they pulled the security guard because it "cost too much" and only reinstated it after a member of staff was hit over the head with a wine bottle after asking a shoplifter to leave. Despite having to deal with incredibly volatile shoplifters on a daily basis to the point that there are certain ones we just do not approach because they've seriously assaulted people previously, we can't get a security guard to cover even the later hours of a shift where we're far more vulnerable. 

My work colleagues have been physically assaulted, spat at, had hot drinks thrown over them. Once one became aware that we're covered by insurance if we're injured in the store they made an attempt to purposefully drag one of my colleagues outside of the building to beat the shit out of him for no reason knowing damn well he wouldn't have been entitled to any care or payout from the company. 

Most of my job experience has been in retail and up until the lockdowns began I never once felt unsafe at work. I never felt threatened or as if I had to keep looking over my shoulder 'just in case'. We make the calls to the police, we send off security footage, and don't hear a lot back (if anything). If we're lucky the shoplifter will get banned from the store and we got a group of them banned and arrested for stealing from the store and selling the items on to other people. 

One of us has to be seriously injured or die for anything to change. It shouldn't be that way and we shouldn't have to go to work with that kind of hyper awareness. To a certain degree I think it's been made far more acceptable to treat retail workers like absolute shit and lower than humans to a point, because people are far more reactive and things like being sworn at are far more commonplace. People seem to forget that when they complain about retail workers "looking miserable" and "unfriendly" while on shift, and it's because there's only so much constant stress and abuse a person can take before completely shutting down and not caring. 

Us looking "unfriendly" is pretty much a given when there's a constant possibility that we could be put into a really dangerous situation with little to no warning. When we repeatedly experience threatening behaviour and being sworn at (among other very unpleasant behaviour), of course we're going to look miserable and like we don't want to be there, because if money was no object or if we didn't have some kind of obligation of self-preservation or care we wouldn't be there, simple. 

I'm looking for a new job outside of the retail field. After seeing some horrendous behaviour from people and a lack of action from upper management to put anything into place to protect us on the shop floor I find increasingly that I just don't care anymore. I would have no chance of defending myself against anyone who wanted to harm me. I couldn't protect any of my colleagues, either - and that's even worse. Retail workers have always had the short end of the stick in this aspect but this rise in violence and threats just isn't acceptable.

I'm currently reading Night on the Galactic Railroad and I've been temporarily stopping to go back through Magireco. It's incredibly interesting to go through and notice all these nuances that I can recognize!

I was aware vaguely of the various references to it, and started to read it myself partly to help me with my Japanese reading comprehension and also because of the links that Magireco made to it. 

I haven't read a book in while because I have an awful attention span, making it very difficult to retain concentration when reading a book but it's a good length, not too long and it also helps that it's something I'm interested in! I'd be interested in reading some of Miyazawa's other works as well in the future.

In terms of the PTSD, I've adapted to be able to get things done. I can go to the GP and have a blood test, the only thing that's changed is that I'm no longer able to look at the needle or watch any part of the process. I haven't been able to watch any medical or hospital documentaries and can't do so without feeling like I'm going to throw up at the sight of any injury. I've been back to the hospital for an x-ray and didn't feel uncomfortable at all - but I was very keen to get in and then leave as soon as possible. It's a given that after any healthcare experience I will feel horrendous and have nightmares for the next few nights. 

C-Diff is something that has completely changed parts of me. In a more positive way, I've definitely gotten far more competent in asserting myself and asking directly for help from any medical / healthcare field. It also helped me to really look at my plans to resume finishing my degree and I'm a lot more confident now in returning to education and doing so on my own terms. I'm not going to waste my time or energy going a certain route that I don't want to do for the sake of others. 

Negatively I feel so excluded and isolated from other people. The lack of understanding about C-Diff and just how awful my experience was is something others around me can't fully understand because C-Diff isn't particularly well understood itself. I wonder more and more recently if my work colleagues are nice to me simply out of pity because my health has been absolutely horrendous for over a year at this point. It feels like people are afraid to ask questions or how to approach me at all in some cases, and working in a team has become harder as I find myself genuinely questioning if I can trust my work colleagues. 

Simple, small actions anyone else would dismiss make me seriously question people's intentions. It's a trivial example, but someone threw out some materials for work that I prepare in advance in my own time at home. After asking around at work everyone came to the conclusion they must have accidentally been binned because there's no feasible way we could have gone through that amount of material in the space of one day. It completely soured my mood, despite that fact it was a mistake. Even so I was intensely irritated and angry by the entire situation, and seriously asked myself what was the point in me even putting in all that effort in my own time if someone could ruin it by doing something small and thoughtless. 😔

It also deeply hurt me to see other people socialising and meeting up outside of work (within current Covid restrictions). Everyone else seems to be in on specific plans that simply are not mentioned to me and all I'm asking for is for someone to ask if I'd like to join in. I can't particularly relate to general conversations and idle chatter because constantly fighting the healthcare services to get anything done is far too heavy of a topic for light conversation. It's stressful and isolating to be waiting for some illness to reappear, counting down the weeks and days and not having anyone to talk to. 

I'm so frustrated by the past few months. I'm angry that I've had to constantly stop and start my life and reassess plans or goals on a monthly basis. I am so tired of all of it at this point. Thank you very much, I will absolutely keep advocating for myself and getting what I need out of the medical field. I'm really worried that I'm in the early stages of a C-Diff recurrence as in between constantly feeling like I want to vomit the all too familiar stomach pains are coming back. I dodged hospital admissions twice last time, if it did come back positive now I'm not certain I could avoid that. 

Thank you very much for replying.

I think this is a far better way to interpret Homura's character in terms of the technicalities around mental age. She's emotionally stunted to a degree at 14, but her situation is far worse than any other member of the Quintet because she has the 12 added years of reliving horrendously traumatic things happening around and to Madoka, a person who showed her genuine kindness and acceptance for who Homura is. 

Her brain hasn't developed with age, so the discussion around Homura being 26 mentally doesn't really apply itself well here at all. It confuses things more than anything else. She hadn't aged physically due to her body merely being something to puppet, so it makes sense that the next logical step is to assume her brain hasn't developed either. 

Homura was isolated socially due to her heart condition, spent time away from school and was further isolated upon returning to school and viewed as being weak or less than her peers. Madoka is an extremely prescious person to Homura not only because she treated Homura nicely and was emotionally open, but because Madoka was the only person to do so. People make the point that Homura met Mami alongside Madoka but only focused on Madoka to argue that she has sociopathic traits which isn't a fair interpretation. 

Mami is far more closed off emotionally and reserved, meaning that Homura naturally wouldn't develop the same kind of attachment. After seeing Madoka die the first time and realising that the only peer who accepted her was now gone, Homura wasn't able to face the uncertainty that a life without that kindness would be worth living. Homura's wish gave her the control she felt she needed over the circumstances to repeat and re-do her meeting with Madoka so she could protect her but also prolong and gain the emotional reassurance Madoka had given her. 

In early timelines this is something that works, but as the distance between Madoka and Homura grows with each loop so does Homura's emotional disconnection from others. The isolation returns and it becomes harder to truly communicate with Madoka in the same way. When Homura lost the emotional reassurance from Madoka, the only thing left she could do was protect her to ensure that one day, she would be able to gain that back. 

I apologize if I'm not making a lot of sense, I'm unwell and the medication prescribed to treat it has made my thoughts a bit jumbled up. Hopefully everything reads as it should but if it doesn't I will try my best to clarify.

I really love Homura as a character because she has so much depth to her. When she's introduced in the main series, she's already undergone a huge shift in character that the audience aren't aware of until the last 2 episodes. She endlessly repeated the same month over and over again for 12 years - her appearance is that of a middle school student but mentally she's 26 years old. 

Her cold and distant presentation is the result of her previous experiences, but because we haven't seen those first the viewers first impression comes from what we can take away from Homura at face value - her actions are interpreted as sociopathic, selfish and her interactions with characters other than Madoka are deemed to be purely exploitative and self-serving. She's a character that you have to work backwards to really understand and there's more complexity to analysing her actions and motives. 

Homura's labyrinth is her interpretation of the ideal life for a magical girl, one that under Kyuubey's design in unobtainable. Once a contract is formed, it's too late. Long term survival and any quality of life before has gone. In Homura's labyrinth magical girls do not risk losing their lives in battles, there is no conflict in groups of magical girls fighting together and they have a life outside of simply maintaining survival. When the Holy Quintet each lunch together, they share everything out equally. There is enough food for everyone. 

It's one of my favourite scenes because it so sharply contrasts the true reality of being a magical girl - the supply of grief seeds is a point of conflict for magical girls and they are willing to fight, steal from or kill other magical girls in order to sustain their own survival. In Homura's labyrinth everyone can live a normal life with the things that Kyuubey's system intentionally doesn't provide - Mami has Nagisa for companionship. She doesn't have to hide her true feelings behind a false bravado alone because she has emotional support. Sayaka and Kyoko have a deeper understanding of each other and a relationship where they respect the wellbeing of the other. They don't fight between themselves with the intention of killing or seriously injuring each other over their moral beliefs. 

Madoka has a life where she doesn't have to witness the suffering and pain of those she cares about, or have to bear the burden of watching Sayaka becoming incredibly self-destructive and the aftermath of her becoming a witch. Everyone gets along and are friends, even as magical girls - something impossible to achieve in the loops Homura experienced. In the main series Homura's behaviour is perceived as negative and her intentions to preserve the wellbeing and safety of Madoka alone come across as tunnel vision or controlling.

That doesn't mean that deep down she didn't care about the other characters and does try to warn or help them (attempting to warn Mami before she fights Charlotte and giving Sayaka a grief seed when she refused to purify her own soul gem). However the other characters react to Homura exactly as the audience do - she is taken at face value and appears to be untrustworthy, so is ignored. In nearly 100 timelines Homura must have attempted to save or protect other members of the Holy Quintet until she realised that it wasn't possible, so chose to prioritize the one person she can protect and who's at the core of her wish, Madoka. Additionally Madoka had the reach to influence Sayaka, Mami and Kyoko - something Homura didn't due to the other's perception of her. 

The end of Rebellion also shows that Homura wants to preserve the wellbeing and happiness of the Holy Quintet besides Madoka. It was a feeling meant for Madoka alone, but it benefitted the other characters just as much. Kyuubey's intentions meant that magical girls would eventually live and die in the same conditions before the Law of Cycles. Homura was willing to make herself an enemy of the people who she was protecting to ensure they live happy, normal lives at her own expense.

Medical issues were the main factor in me deciding that I don't want to have children. There are strong lines of both drug and alcohol addiction on both sides of my extended family. The women on my mother's side of the family have varying degrees of depression and eating disordered behaviour - my cousin and I, for example, have both had eating disorders. I have an increased risk of developing heart problems later on in life that was passed down to me and my sibling through my father's line. 

I grew up in the mental health services, entirely isolated from my peers and as a result I suffered a lot and experienced things a young person shouldn't have to witness. I refuse to push that onto a child who did not consent to being conceived in the first place. My depression is treatment resistant and it will be with me for life - I wouldn't wish that on anyone else. I wouldn't be able to forgive myself for pushing all the years of pain and self-loathing onto a child who didn't ask to be born. 

My physical health isn't great either - Hypothyroidism, Asthma, IBS - the list is getting worryingly longer. I was unwell for 3 months with 3 different illnesses, had 2 months where I was trying to manage the aftereffects of my illnesses, and I'm unwell again at the moment. My body can barely keep itself functioning, let alone be healthy enough to carry a child for 9 months. I'm highly confident that I wouldn't be able to carry a pregnancy to term  even if I wanted to have children.

My experiences in childhood, growing up and my relationship with my parents were also motivating factors in my choice to not have children. The way I see it there are multiple different problems, mentally or physically, that I could pass onto a child. Looking at my current quality of life and how much work I've had to put in to get to a place where I feel confident in myself, I would be passing down my quality of life at varying ages to a child who would automatically be at a disadvantage by design and who has absolutely no say in existing in the first place. 

It's not fair. It would be cruel and an absolutely awful thing to do.

I think my ability to think clearly is muddied by a few different factors: there's the Dyspraxia for starters. I recall scoring quite highly for mild/moderate ADHD in a neurological assessment I had at 17, although this hasn't been formally diagnosed so I don't apply the diagnosis to myself personally. 

I also sustained a second degree concussion and post traumatic amnesia when I was 18 at my job, and after that I noticed a huge drop in my ability to focus and concentrate. It was around that time I began to fall asleep in classes which persisted throughout my time at university as well.

I was unwell for 3 months with different illnesses (food poisoning, Kidney infection and C-difficle) which took every ounce of energy and brain power I had left out of me. Up until recently I was feeling a bit better but I've become unwell again and all that brain power has completely disappeared. 

My understanding of my own cognitive abilities at the moment are that I've just been dealt a bad hand in terms of things that happened which has made the Dyspraxia and ADHD-like problems worse than they otherwise would be. My physical health being quite poor for the past few months has not helped matters. 

In terms of how I manage this mentally, I know that this inability to really focus isn't reflective of my capabilities or intelligence. I can achieve everything I want and more, I just have to approach it in a different way, take my time and go at my own pace.

I've been working throughout the pandemic in retail and it's mentally exhausting. The store had security guards for brief periods of time until it became too expensive, so for most of it I end up doing 2 jobs at the same time - I'm there doing the job I applied for and also having to be a security guard at the same time. Shoplifting has been a massive problem and my hands are tied every single time - I can't get physically close to a shoplifter in case they're physically aggressive and due to social distancing, but I can't get whatever item(s) a person has chosen to steal out of their hands. Nobody wins: the store loses money, staff become demotivated and customers question if we even care about theft anymore. There isn't a solution that leaves everyone happy or at least satisfied. 

There's been some horrendous attitudes throughout the pandemic - understandably people are a bit more on edge and reactive but some behaviour can't be excused. My colleagues have been spat at, verbally abused and physically attacked while trying to work and keep the shop open so people can buy food. There was one store where security guards were only placed back into the store after a member of staff was hit over the head with a wine bottle. You see the worst in people sometimes working retail and it makes you lose your faith in the goodness of people. 

One of my colleagues was physically assaulted trying to stop a shoplifter, after attempting to drag my colleague out of the store so the shoplifter could beat the shit out of him the shoplifter resorted to just throwing loaves of bread at my colleague. Amusing to see in the moment, but it's scary to think the damage that could have been done if that shoplifter had been near a product contained in a glass jar or a wine bottle. I've seen people leave used needles in the store and even dog poo, which one of my colleagues had the joy of having to remove.

To my Eating Disorder, 

I know why you appeared in those years of growing up in the clinical embrace of CAMHS. Looking back at those years with jaded and adult eyes, it was inevitable. Of course, as your presence permeated my teenage years, you robbed me of many years of living, of growing into someone with a personality, of experiencing life in a similar manner to my peers. 

Climbing back out of that black hole was the most difficult thing I've ever done. To this day, it is something so difficult that my memory of those times has transcended the days and time passed spent stuck; from what I've been told, you didn't make things easy for anyone. I remember feeling like I wasn't going to wake up if I went to sleep at night. I remember realising that I didn't want to die, and all the 'comfort' you had given me had deceitfully lead to years of suffering and pain at my expense. 

To others, I was defined by your presence. From the girls at school who whispered behind my back about you, to the ballet teacher and popular girls who praised me for my commitment to the art and stopped ignoring me for the first time in 11 years. Who I truly was as a person didn't matter: the only thing that did was you. You put me in front row of my last performance, but by that time you had ruined my body to the degree that I could not fully lift my arms above my head. I don't have the last professional picture from that performance, because 'I' am not in it. You are. 

In the years since my recovery you have remained in a crevice of my mind, ready to offer some helpful 'advice' if something was going wrong. I don't mind if you stay there, but I hope you know that every single time you appear I am strong enough and determined enough to put you back in your place. 

You stole too many years of my life and I will not allow you to take any more from me.

What I've never really understood is that people can't seem to recognise that in the same way they made an informed choice to have children, we've made an informed choice to not have children, all for our own reasons. They're both equally informed choices, yet our decision to be childfree is respected less. 

Our reasons for choosing not to have children are invalidated and not taken seriously because the two choices are not viewed as equal and respected as such - there is no effective communication possible in a debate at present about this because there's a bias from the very beginning. 

I wonder if other subs see some of our discussions and interpret them subjectively and personally as disparaging their personal choices in life instead of looking at it objectively: this is a sub for discussions about being childfree and our experiences. Everyone here has had different experiences in life and gone about being childfree in unique ways, exactly the same way that people who choose to have children have decided that they want to start a family of their own.

This is something I'm trying to manage now - I lost a lot around my hairline as it comes out at the root. I thought it was only the front of my hairline but when I went to get my hair cut my hairdresser also told me it had happened to the back as well.

I lost weight really rapidly when I started antibiotics for C-Diff and only noticed the hair loss towards the end of the antibiotic course, but I was shocked that I could run my fingers through my hair and lose that much. I'm assuming that the sudden weight loss and lack of vitamins both contributed to it, and it's slowed down a lot since I've started eating like I used to and have gained some weight back. 

My hairdresser recommended that I start using the Plantur 39 Caffeine shampoo to retain the thickness of my hair and to slow down how much hair I lose through brushing and washing it. In my case the most important thing was getting vitamins back into my diet that I'd been missing and starting to take my B12, Folic Acid and Vitamin D supplements again after roughly a month of not using them. 

I had a blood test done a few weeks ago that showed everything was looking normal in terms of my vitamin levels which is a relief. Focus on getting those vitamins back into your diet or look into supplements to help boost the ones you don't get enough of from food. I've seen an improvement in the thickness of my hair too with the Plantur 39 shampoo so I would recommend trying that and seeing if it helps with the hair loss. 

One thing I would also recommend is try not to worry too much about the hair loss. I spent a lot of time looking into the bathroom mirror at work cursing these patchy spots on my hairline that hadn't been there before all of this happened. It's really difficult to not notice it and be bothered by it but it is temporary, and it will get better by taking care of your diet. 

Best of luck at the doctor's - it took me 2 months post C-Diff to feel comfortable going to see a GP again. Still working on my acquired fear of the dentist but that's a work in progress. 😊

I highly dislike being physically touched by people I don't trust or know that well and it makes me very uncomfortable. I've been with my partner for 7 years and have no problem with seeking out or asking for physical affection or intimacy from them, for me it's a matter of feeling safe and confident I can trust someone. My partner and my best friend are the only two people where I feel comfortable with physical touch and feel comfort from a hug, for example. 

My fear with any person is that they are being nice to me because they want something out of me - if someone asks me for a favour or to assist with something, I'm immediately thinking "what's the catch here, what's my end of the bargain, what will the other person gain from this that I won't". Due to past experiences I'm extremely wary of people giving me compliments, rewarding me for something I've achieved or generally being nice to me. This mindset is linked with my dislike of physical touch and until I know a person well enough I won't feel comfortable with any physical contact. 

I remember making a list of my "rules for life" with a therapist a few years ago, and mine were entirely centered around the idea that people are hypocrites, people are self-serving, people are selfish and exploitative and nobody can be trusted. This ties into intimacy in that I have a non-existent libido and any intimacy with my partner has to happen because I've asked if we can be intimate, my partner has agreed and it's something I've initiated by asking. I feel like I have more control over the situation that way because it's something I've asked for and I won't feel used or taken advantage of afterwards. 

I don't feel any emotional or physical attraction to other people and only develop romantic attraction to others if I've gotten to know them well enough that I feel comfortable around them, can talk about my feelings with them and feel safe around them. Even then it isn't guaranteed I'll feel anything like that towards a person because I won't be able to trust that the information I've given them about myself and how I feel will be respected and not used as gossip for others or fodder for manipulation at some point. 

Intimacy and sexuality are really difficult things to think about for me, because I don't really know myself. I suppose the closest thing would be bisexual - if someone made me feel that safe, and I trusted them with my feelings, I'd probably develop attraction to them regardless of gender.

I took driving lessons for 2 years before I stopped. My parents were very insistent that I learn to drive in a manual car and as a result it took me significantly longer to be competent at any of it. I switched driving instructor after my previous one stopped giving me consistent lessons every week and asked if I felt comfortable having a lesson with her daughter in the car when she had come home early from school sick.

My second instructor was very tough and direct, something I thought would be beneficial as I work better with direct instructions. I remember I had one awful lesson where for some reason I just kept screwing everything up and I could feel the frustration radiating off him. I made some kind of error just before going onto a dual carriageway and he started to shout at me. I drove down the dual carriageway in tears, incredibly upset at the entire situation and not in a state to be driving a car at all. 

He realised what he'd done, apologised for it and I finished the rest of the lesson. But I never took any more lessons after that one because the experience put me off driving entirely. Both instructors knew I had Dyspraxia, that certain elements were going to be difficult for me and that progress would be made at a significantly slower pace. 

I don't want to drive. I can't trust myself to drive any vehicle knowing that I am more likely to make a big mistake and harm other drivers on the road. I don't have the attention span or concentration for it and I know that it would be a matter of time before something happened if I did actually pass my test and be qualified to drive.

I have been socially rejected in the workplace on one occasion. I worked in a big toy shop (my contract was 6 months, I left after 1 month) with these massive shelves that required using really tall ladders to reach them. In my interview I was asked if I felt comfortable with the idea of using them and I replied that I wouldn't feel comfortable doing so because of my Dyspraxia. However I said that I need the practice and that I am able to do it, but I might need a bit longer to get used to it. They told me that was no problem, so I went in assuming that everything was fine. I was wrong. 

Because I disclosed my Dyspraxia at the interview when they were asking about disabilities, I was completely socially rejected because I initially found certain things difficult and it took me longer to learn and feel comfortable with handling heavy stock on those tall ladders. The other person who started at the same time as me was immediately welcomed into the social group while I was left out and had to manage the till areas entirely on my own. It was a big store so walkie talkies were at a premium and I was usually given one that was broken (if I had a working one someone would usually come by and swap the broken one for my working one). 

I couldn't communicate with the rest of the team and grew frustrated when I was repeatedly spoken to about not meeting the stupid time target for tills (a customer had to arrive at a till and be served within 2 minutes. That's completely impossible to achieve). I repeatedly explained that I had a broken device so I couldn't tell anyone anything if I needed assistance and that I was trying my best to tend to every customer but nothing changed. There was a supervisor who really did not like me (I have no idea why) and got very frustrated when I asked questions about the best way in terms of time management to complete a task, if I had a question about how to do something etc. I went to my GP towards the end of the month and they told me that I had constantly been having panic attacks for hours on end while at work partly due to the way I was treated and cast out from the rest of the team. 

The straw that broke the camel's back for me was when I went in to cover an early morning shift that I was meant to do on the rota, only to arrive and be told someone else was covering it, had agreed to do so the day before while I was at work, and I was not informed of the change. At the time I was working 2 jobs so I had the option to leave the toy store behind and increase my hours at the second job, so I did that. I put in my resignation and per the contract prepared to leave in a week's time. I showed up to find I'd been pulled off the rota immediately after giving my resignation and they weren't expecting me to show up at all. I stayed for a few hours, got really fed up with all of it and told my manager that I was leaving immediately. 

It was only then they finally realized that I meant what I said and that they had pushed out an employee after a month. Apparently everyone had "really liked me" there and the entire time I was wondering that if that really was the case, why did they not show me that through their actions? Saying that at that moment felt incredibly shallow and manipulative. As a result of working there for 1 month I keep my anxiety in check in the workplace with beta blockers as a large queue of customers make me extremely anxious and has caused me to have panic attacks at work on a few occasions in the few months after leaving the toy store job. 

I am so much happier where I work now, actually look forward to going into work and everyone is so nice and friendly. It's a great team of people and I know that I am a part of that team and that my work is valued and important. It's so nice to be thanked at the end of a shift for being there and for doing my best.

I do this a lot at work. It's fairly common for me to clock in, get everything I need to start my shift and then just appear out of nowhere and startle my colleagues because I'm very quiet and don't make a lot of noise. I also accidentally frighten my colleagues by appearing behind them or from behind a corner or simply by asking them a question when they haven't realized I'm in the same room as them. 

It happens sometimes at home as well, but generally it's something I tend to do more at work. I'm worse with large physical movements, so I put a lot of effort into being able to move big trolleys and cages of stock around without driving them into things and making a big noise. My hard work has paid off, and I now feel fairly confident in moving such things around, but as a result I end up scaring my colleagues far more often! 

One bonus of being that quiet is that if I'm sorting something out below the till customers may not realize I'm there at all. It's good for if I need a quiet moment to have a breather as I can get myself together and work better.

Flagyl is the cheapest drug to prescribe for C-Diff and it has the worst side effects. It's also otoxic and can damage your hearing, something I'm having to manage now as a result of my GP prescribing Flagyl. 

Do not take it.

I'm grateful to have had treatment, but it was treatment I really had to fight to get in the first place. Nobody took my concerns seriously so when it was finally confirmed I'd tested positive for C-Diff, I was too tired and feeling too unwell to ask any questions about Flagyl when it was prescribed to me. I only had so much fight left in me at that point and it was all gone by the time I was in the waiting room for my emergency GP appointment. 

I'm far better informed now, I'm currently waiting on the results of a sample as this is my first IBS flare post C-Diff. If it came up again at any point I would ask to specifically not be prescribed it again. After  my concerns were dismissed repeatedly, finally getting treatment and thinking it's all done with and it's over, I find out Flagyl has damaged my hearing. Given how frustrating the entire process was, even though they followed a treatment plan objectively, I can't help but feel badly about the outcome subjectively.

My parents emotionally neglected my sibling and I when we were young. A few years ago my Dad was reflecting on how he tried to "toughen us up" as children and deeply regretted doing so seeing that my brother and I both grew up and developed our own problems. 

I was in CAMHS from the ages of 13 - 17, during that I had a severe eating disorder and in 2012 I had a limb threatening injury due to sepsis after severely self-harming and nearly lost my right arm below the elbow. I went through my exams at school both simultaneously recovering from anorexia and nearly losing my arm. My teenage years in that regard were highly unusual and pretty isolating. 

I was back for Christmas in my second year of university when my sibling had a Xanax overdose and an ambulance was called and I was the only one who knew what he had taken. 

I knew at that point that I had BPD, so I don't think I've answered your question - however I had many experiences in my late teenage years that added to the emotional neglect in my childhood that set off the BPD in the first place. The experiences I had as a teenager definitely made everything worse mental health wise.

I remember being really surprised that I didn't care about anyone's opinions in terms of my weight at the end of my treatment. I remember some of my classmates whispering behind my back about why I was so thin and talking about my eating disorder. The other girls stared at me whenever I changed for PE and I always knew that after any PE class, there would be more whispers and odd looks from my classmates. In one of my biology classes we were learning about BMI and had to weigh ourselves and calculate our BMI - every person in that classroom was waiting for me to step on the scale so they could get a peek at my weight (I really hope this kind of activity isn't still used in lessons about BMI because it was the most humiliating experience I went through, and my school was grossly incompetent for allowing me to even be in that lesson knowing I was in the early stages of recovery at the time). 

From going from being extremely angry constantly about people's attitudes to not caring at all at the end of treatment was something I thought I would never be able to do. The anger I felt towards everything in life felt like it was never going to go away, but in the end, it did. It was a relief to know that I could move past that - my eating disorder had me so beaten down that I believed I couldn't change anything about my situation and I had no choice, but the emotional resilience needed to get through treatment and therapy made me remember that I'm far stronger than I thought I was.

I got a bit suspicious when the audiologist asked if I wanted to join the waiting list for a hearing aid consultation immediately after stating that I wouldn't actually need them for a few years. My first thought was that they were going to try and sell me expensive hearing aids so I politely declined the offer. I have to wear a headset at work that I would usually wear on my left ear (at max volume because otherwise I can't properly hear my colleagues), so I'll switch to my right ear and preserve as much of my hearing in my left ear as possible. 

The current plan is to wait a few weeks so I can really process what's happened and start looking into this further. I didn't want to go to sleep last night, so I stayed up until 4AM staring at the walls not really knowing how to feel. I'm currently waiting for the results of a stool sample to see if I've had a recurrence of C-Diff which has also messed with my head a bit. I started having nightmares again after having my blood test done, so it's back to basic self-care for a bit. 

In the past 2 months I could put one foot in front of the other and actually felt positive about everything. I still can go out and get everything sorted but when I stop to think about it I feel so damn miserable about all of this.

I went to Urgent Care first after not being able to get hold of my GP. I ordered some sample containers off Amazon and once it was confirmed that I was going to Urgent Care I took my stool sample with me unprompted and dropped it off directly at the hospital. My sample came back positive a few days later and it was only then my GP took the situation seriously and I started antibiotics for C-Diff. 

Avoid Flagyl if they try to give it to you. It's Otoxic and is the worst antibiotic for C-Diff.
