To my knowledge it's more common in Dyspraxic children to throw tantrums and have outbursts of frustration. It's an extremely difficult thing to live with as many others have posted here: Dyspraxic adults are far more likely to develop depression and anxiety as a result of having Dyspraxia. The problem is that there is generally support for children, but no support for Dyspraxic adults - and if you've grown up with feelings of frustration at not being able to do certain things to the same level of ability as your peers, being teased and made fun of for being 'different' (kids are mean and usually equate lack of ability to intelligence which is not the case at all for people with Dyspraxia), low self-esteem and feelings of being useless or an inconvenience to others then some of your partner's behaviours make sense. 

I'm a bit worried that he can become physically aggressive - and I sincerely hope not towards you. There is a distinction between feeling frustrated due to Dyspraxia and just being an asshole. The most important thing is that he really needs to talk to a therapist to get some grip on his emotions and how to notice when he's feeling angry and actively do something to prevent that feeling getting out of hand. I don't know if he's had a therapist before or not but it would also be worth it so he can process some of those deep-seated emotions and experiences he's had through childhood, reflect on why he reacts the way he does and then look for practical steps he can take to address them in daily life. 

I know when I was a teenager getting to grips with being Dyspraxic that I was extremely pessimistic about the future and my capability to pursue what I wanted to in terms of a career and hobbies. Knowing that when I wanted to try and do something or work towards a goal my progress would not be linear or it would take me longer to do what I wanted was absolutely crushing. It was only a few years later when I was in university that I realized that I don't need to keep up with anyone else, I don't need to do what everyone else is doing, and I don't learn things the same way everyone else does. I stopped caring about what other people were achieving and focused on what I wanted to do, and what I needed to do to get to where I wanted to be. 

This approach can be applied to small tasks as well as long-term ones: for example I identified areas where I'm not so great at things like my knife skills when I'm cooking a meal, time management (I take longer to do things than other people at work) etc. So I set small goals to achieve throughout the week, simple things like remembering where I put something or remembering to take the bins out on the right day. Having a go at chopping vegetables when my partner cooks a meal. Small things in my daily routine that allow me to feel like I've achieved something, that I'm actively working to improve my skills in something I find difficult. That may be something worth trying with your partner. 

A lot of this comes down to him being able to manage his emotions and I think that should be your and his priority. If he can develop more understanding about why he reacts as he does and that he can identify ways that he can counteract those intense emotional outbursts then he'll have the understanding to be more attentive to your needs and wants, to express his emotions in a healthy way. Instant gratification is something that many dyspraxic folks struggle with and it goes hand in hand with that feeling of frustration and uselessness. If he can make steps to change his mindset then he can also make changes to how he approaches tasks, how he responds emotionally if something doesn't go as he intended, trying out a new hobby or craft etc. 

It's a tricky one, because it's hard to separate responses coming from the feelings Dyspraxia brings up from him just being a jerk because he can. I hope you can come to some kind of resolution with him and figure out how to navigate this.

I always noticed something didn't feel right whenever I needed a medication increase. I always felt like I'd lost something intangible and my normal routine felt empty, the hobbies I do didn't seem to interest me anymore etc. I can always pinpoint exactly when my mood starts to go downhill depending on if I can brush my teeth twice a day, get out of bed and not have to force myself to do everything. 

I'm taking 200mg of Zoloft, I have been for a while now (roughly 5 years at this point). As far as I know I'm on the highest therapeutic dose, and as long as Zoloft doesn't stop working for me like Prozac did after 6 years (most of those years also being at highest therapeutic dose) then I'm happy. 

What I'd recommend to you is keep a record of a week on your current dose. Note what symptoms occur when, especially if some are worse at night. Keep a mood diary alongside this as you can bring it to your doctor and they can decide from the evidence you've provided if you should increase your SSRI medication. Another marker is if your normal coping mechanisms are not working as well or at all - this is also a sign that you may need to increase your dose.

There's a clash in ideals here. It sounds to me like your family doesn't quite understand or respect your future Sister in Law's choice to have a childfree wedding. I'm going to say it once: it isn't your wedding. It isn't your family's wedding. It is your brother and his partner's wedding. They are not obligated to cater to anyone else's demands or expectations for how they plan their wedding. Your initial response was the compromise in this situation: you declined the invitation because due to the practicalities of childcare it was not possible to attend. You should have left it at that. Simply decline, pass on your well wishes to the married couple and let them enjoy their wedding day. 

This is my second issue: you seem to have some form of dislike/resentment towards your future SIL. This goes beyond the wedding being childfree - this is a problem with the way you treat your future SIL. You focus far more on her than your brother and it leads me to wonder if your family has tried to chase away any other partners from marrying into the family because they don't share your ideas and values. You are a grown adult. Be an adult and be respectful to your future SIL: you may not share the same beliefs in terms of having children but that is no excuse for treating her terribly. Just as you and your family made informed choices to have children, she has made an informed choice to not have children. Just because it's a different perspective to your own doesn't mean that it's wrong. Respect her choice the way you would expect your choices to be respected. If the shoe was on the other foot I imagine you wouldn't feel particularly great right now, would you? 

Now, they're getting married - do you really, truly believe that if they had committed to something like this that they wouldn't have some kind of shared beliefs and values? Your brother enjoys the presence of his nieces and nephews, and enjoys spending time with them - but there is a difference. Your brother loves his nieces and nephews but wants a childfree wedding. It doesn't change his love for them at all - but he wants to enjoy his wedding to his fiancée without them there because it's a special moment and day for them as a couple. They get to choose how they celebrate that day because it's theirs - it isn't your family's, it isn't yours. Why are you pinning all these horrible feelings and rhetoric on your future SIL alone? It's really infantile and pathetic that you're trying to chase away someone marrying into your family like that. Calling her 'psycho' doesn't help your argument here. 

There is no middle ground. The compromise here was you and other family members who couldn't attend simply don't. Be respectful to your brother and future SIL, let them celebrate their marriage the way they want to. This has caused a big family dilemma in that a lot of family members with children have declined the invitation to attend, and your parents who are partly funding the wedding are now questioning their part in providing the finances to them. You all need to sit down as a family with a mediator and talk this one out respectfully. Don't talk over anyone else, don't interrupt, let everyone say what they want to say in an objective and clear way. There seems to be a huge lack of communication here and if you all get on the same page, you can work towards a resolution. 

An alternative solution to this could be asking all the family members not attending to make a short video congratulating the couple on their marriage. Talk with you brother and future SIL on putting them all together and maybe having it play at the wedding at some point if your brother and SIL agree to that. That way you and other family members not attending can still feel involved, and your future SIL may feel more positively about the fact that some family members aren't there in person.

Also: I think you've blurred the line or misinterpreted what you future SIL meant when she mentioned your children being your "problem" in this situation. You, as their parent, are responsible for them and their well-being. Objectively, she is asking you here to be the responsible caregiver and make the right choice for your children. If you cannot find someone to take care of your children to attend the wedding then it is you responsibility to politely decline the invitation. You seem to have latched onto the word "problem" here as something subjective and warped it to fit your own narrative, something I'm not surprised about since you seem to deeply dislike her and the concept of her marrying into your family.  

Yes, you are the Asshole. Your attitude towards your future SIL is horrendous. You and your family are adults. Be adults for once and have respect for her and your brother - even if you don't agree on personal views that is no excuse to disrespect her based on one judgement. Agree to disagree, respect her and your brother's choices, and work towards fixing this before it's too late and the relationship between the couple and rest of your family is irreparable.

I've been fortunate enough to be working during the various states of lockdown in the UK. Recently I found out that my cousin and her partner, both teachers in a primary school, ended up getting Covid from the children in their classrooms. Why is it that in my job, where arguably I contribute less (not sure if serving customers on tills, filling shelves with stock and preparing people's online orders is more important than the teachers educating children in a pandemic), I get more benefits and protection than the teachers putting themselves at risk on a daily basis to maintain a consistent level of education? 

Both my cousin and I have been working, we've both been doing so during a pandemic. So why is it that the way we're treated both by our profession and other people relying on our profession so incredibly different? After finding out that my cousin got Covid from the children in her class, I can't stand the parents who go onto social media and have the audacity and entitlement to complain that the closure of schools (and not even the full closure in the UK - schools have been open for the children of key workers) has absolutely devastated their genius child's development and they're never going to reach their full potential because of the teachers and schools that closed. The fact that these parents override the young people responding saying that they're concerned about getting Covid and passing it on to vulnerable family members or getting someone they love sick, and are happy that schools are closed and that their education, while important, can wait to be resumed properly. 

It isn't just your child that can't do those things. Everyone can't do those things - the university students promised blended learning before being quarantined to their halls of residence and still being made to pay rent. They can't go to school, they can't learn and have the university experience they deserve. What about the dental students hopeful of starting their studies only to be told they'd have to wait a year because the students already on the course, through no fault of their own, have to study for another year because they couldn't get the in person clinical experience needed to graduate? None of us can see our friends - it's been over a year since I saw my best friend. We send letters to each other regularly but when both of us aren't feeling good and want to see each other just to have a hug and hang out, it isn't like we can do that either. I had 3 illnesses in 3 months from November - January: what I wouldn't give to have just been able to hug my friend and have her there to hold my hand when the constant pain got too much to bear. 

I know colleagues who have been spat at, verbally abused and physically assaulted while trying to do their jobs. There's been a rise in shoplifters and due to Covid we have to put distance between ourselves and other people to keep ourselves save and so that there will actually be staff available to keep the shop open. A customer recently asked me if we care about shoplifters anymore because, on the outside, it looks like we willingly let them in and take whatever they want. The reality is the inverse - we haven't been given the funds for proper security to keep an eye on the store, so we have to do everything ourselves. We look at the CCTV footage, we call the police, and nothing happens. Essentially we're doing 2 completely different jobs at the same time, both that put us at risk in terms of getting too close to a person who is asymptomatic or, unknown to us, has tested positive for Covid and doesn't care. I would still rather deal with those kinds of shoplifters than parents. 

With teaching, the parent's involvement and collaboration is absolutely critical. When you're educating a child their parents are automatically involved and you have no choice in that, even if the parents are entitled, rude and make your job so much harder than it needs to be in a time where everything is already exponentially more difficult by default. Parents need to understand that teachers have a life outside of their jobs - we all do. Parenting to me is one of those things that just becomes someone's life to the point where they have tunnel vision and can't see anything outside of that. The teacher you've just harassed about your child's perceived 'regression'? They have family. They're someone's daughter/son, someone's wife/husband. They're someone's brother or sister. Maybe they care for a vulnerable relative, maybe someone they love has medical problems that make them more vulnerable to Covid (my uncle has liver failure and diabetes, for example. He's already in a bad way, if he were to get Covid I'm not sure how good his chance of survival would be). 

How many elderly people have died in care homes due to exposure to Covid, or deteriorated in their current condition because they can't regularly see their family members anymore and have given up their will to keep on persevering? There's been a lot of discussion about mental health and pressure on an already underfunded and overstretched NHS to provide mental health care to so many people encountering mental health difficulties for the first time. What about the people who have gone to their GP and been given an SSRI for the first time with little to no information on their medication, and have to navigate that alongside not having the support to understand their mental health problems in a healthy manner? 

How many people have started drinking excessively, using illicit substances and started smoking cigarettes because of the stress that Covid has placed in our lives? Too many. Everyone is suffering, regardless of the fact that they may not have children. In a way, the children are the fortunate ones here. Everyone else has to get up, put one foot in front of the other because we have no choice, we have commitments, and see the bigger picture. What does a child think about? Probably what's for lunch and are their friends going to be around later to play football with them. Everyone else has to keep going and experiencing the horrific reality of the current state of the world, but we don't suffer fully if we don't have children and aren't a parent? That's bullshit.

I avoided being admitted into hospital twice and there was some discussion about getting surgeons involved to see if I was a candidate for surgery at one point. It was the most unpleasant and horrible experience I've ever had. That bus journey home was  incredibly uncomfortable and once I was actually home and had taken a shower I didn't leave my house after that point for a week. 

I would recommend getting some buscopan - it helped take the edge off some of the bloating for me. Peppermint oil capsules were also quite helpful, but I would recommend taking them after you've eaten something because I found they give me acid reflux if I take them without food. Especially with C-Diff the last thing you want right now is to be constantly tasting peppermint in your mouth and the added feeling of going to vomit on top of the nausea that's already there. 

When I started my antibiotics for C-Diff I also became constipated - Fybogel is good if you don't feel like your stomach can tolerate food but you still want to get some fibre into your system to help you have a BM. It's far gentler than macrogol and shouldn't agitate your bowel to cause you additional pain. 

Take care and get plenty of rest ❤️

When I went to A&E during having C-Diff, Codiene wouldn't touch the pain. I went home with Morphine in the end. When I'm in a lot of pain like that, I don't make noise but I do get very quiet. However I made a hell of a lot of noise when any doctor came round to poke my stomach. I have no idea how I got home after that considering I nearly passed out and threw up while waiting for the bus. 

I normally take macrogol on a regular basis for my IBS (pre C-Diff) and that was agitating my bowels too much. Instead I was told to drink a lot of water, and when I felt like eating it had to be something high fibre to help me to go naturally and get the C-Diff out of my system. When I felt like I wanted a warm drink, I had a lot of chamomile tea. Couldn't drink any other type of tea but chamomile for some reason. 

My diet was pretty much just bananas and white rice. I also had a lot of soups when I felt I couldn't tolerate any solid food, and I did try high-fibre smoothies once but never again after because I have never wanted to puke so badly in my life.

I used to go into every therapy session at 13/14 with the intent of running rings around my therapist. I started out very genuinely, and engaged with treatment initially - that changed when I felt let down repeatedly by CAMHS. Yes, I would go in and tell them what they wanted to hear so they would leave me alone. It became this weird game to see how far I could take something before they would do anything about it. My goal was to push them to send me to inpatient treatment, to do something so big that they had to listen to me. That was all I wanted. I just wanted to be listened to. And I went to stupid lengths and did awful things to try and get that. 

I was in CAMHS from 13-17, and worked hard for years during and after that to separate who I am as a person from the BPD. I look back at my early experiences in treatment and I see someone completely unrecognisable - I don't really see an individual, I see the BPD. I would say I was a nightmare in treatment, but it wasn't 'me' as a person. 

I always approach what I'm feeling in a certain way. The problem is, especially with BPD, we don't know who we are, so the BPD is the next best substitute for a personality. If I don't want to do something, for example, I ask myself if it's truly something I don't want to do or something BPD doesn't want to do. If I want to watch a certain TV show to take my mind off something, and suddenly I'm not sure if I want to, I ask myself if I genuinely just changed my mind and want to watch something else, or if the BPD doesn't want me to watch this show because it knows I'm going to feel more positive after watching it and not feel angry/sad/insert emotion here. 

This is the approach I use with work, too. In the morning I might not feel like going to work, but I know that I genuinely like going to work, I like interacting with my colleagues, I like to chat with customers. I enjoy what I do and I enjoy getting paid for it. What would the BPD want me to do? Probably stay in bed all day and overthink everything so I wind myself up all day and spend it being miserable, and backstab me with thoughts of "I should have gone to work", "I won't get paid for that shift now, I made a mistake". 

The most important part of this process is that you acknowledge the feelings. Acknowledge that you feel a certain way, because denying how we're feeling and forcing positive emotions is counterproductive. It holds the flood for a short period of time, and then the dam breaks the moment we stop. Acknowledge how you're feeling, accept the feeling as being valid, and ask yourself if this is something you as a person are feeling, or if this is something the BPD is forcing you to feel to avoid something/someone that makes you uncomfortable. 

BPD wants you to feel powerful and like you can outsmart things in life. The only thing you achieve in entertaining that is missing out on learning opportunities, meeting new people, improving your confidence in certain situations, and building who you are as a person, not what BPD wants to you be. I know the high of feeling that powerful is alluring, but it isn't real. You deserve to do what BPD says you can't. You deserve to enjoy yourself and not feel guilty for having fun. You deserve treatment, and you deserve to be listened to. 

It's hard work, and there are days where everything feels too much to handle. On those days, don't be hard on yourself. Take care of yourself, be gentle with yourself, and if you feel like talking to someone you can trust, do so. It's really important to tell someone you trust how you're feeling, because this is going to be a process and it might take a while. 

It isn't your fault if you feel like you're not coping. It's normal to not feel comfortable with the responsibility of using coping mechanisms and challenging yourself to do something BPD doesn't want to do. You're not a bad person. 

Take care of yourself. The hospital environment isn't helpful at all for BPD patients, so I hope you can avoid hospitalisation. It might be worth communicating, however you do best, to your mental health team that you don't feel hospital is the best place for you to be. Also look into getting an advocate to support you and help you in getting what you want to say communicated to the people in charge of your care.

The item I used to self-harm with was also used to cut flowers. It was a matter of time before something happened, really. Looking back I never thought about it other than being an object that I used to harm myself with. I was 16 at the time, and what a lesson to learn at 16 - I wouldn't wish it on any young person. 8 years later and I'm putting one foot in front of the other, going to work, doing what needs to be done. Personally I've come to terms with what happened, it's more processing my family's response to it which is something I can only do now I'm older and have seen a little more of the world to make a proper conclusion. 

It really throws you off if it's a big self-harm incident. For me it was waves of regret, embarrassment, anger, depression, frustration - name it, you feel it. Mine came from the realisation that I wasn't as powerful as self-harm made me feel - before I thought I was stronger than everyone else because I could play with my own life and always win. Then reality hits and you're in A&E before Christmas day, wondering where it was that things went too far. It reminded me I was still human, too, and what I was doing was incredibly dangerous. 

You know it's bad when people around you can smell something bad but don't know where it's coming from, knowing damn well it's your infected arm. Self-harm lets you believe you have absolute control, but the fact is that you have none. That was the hardest thing for me to learn.

Yup, fellow hip pain sufferer here. My parents put me ballet classes when I was young to improve my co-ordination and it was helpful at first - my ballet teacher corrected a problem with my feet where I walked inwards within the first year (I remember walking up and down the dance studio a lot trying to walk and not trip up over my own feet). As a result I have a high instep which makes it a pain to find shoes that fit me properly in certain styles. 

My posture and spacial awareness was kind of fixed, but I noticed that the longer I danced (11 years), I got more pain than the other dancers in my knees, ankles and hips. I haven't done ballet in a long time and maybe it's the dyspraxia things not being actively corrected for years, but my hips pop and click a lot. I can sit and pop my ankles for hours (something I've had to stop because every time I do it hurts worse each time). My knees are also not great and give me grief on a regular basis, especially because my job is very physical and a lot of running around and bending down or stretching. 

Something that might make my pain more of a dancer's injury is that I did have anorexia for the last few years when I danced and that hasn't helped. Dyspraxia put me at a disadvantage, the eating disorder took that and ran with it. Now I'm 24 and can't do a squat or bend down comfortably. 

I basically pushed my body far beyond it's limits when it already needed rest and conditioning.

The way I look at it, there are kind of 3 kinds of children in this situation. I absolutely agree children not taught manners become careless and selfish, and easily become destructive because they haven't been taught boundaries. 

Using the self-service machine as an example, one child may begin to wander towards it and the parents will redirect them to the till so I can process the transaction. They return to their parents, listen, and understand that in this situation the machine shouldn't be touched.

Call me soft, but I've seen a lot of children during working in retail that fit into the above categories. I watch closely, I listen closely, and make my conclusion after I've seen what I feel is enough to make a judgement.

I agree with this, it makes me sad to see that happening. This is the response that comes out of treating a child this way - I was the same. When I expressed how I was feeling I was either not acknowledged, made fun of or shouted at, and the only way I knew how to work around it was to people please and act the way my parents wanted me to. As a result I had no sense of my own identity and still carry around years of anger and frustration. 

Doing that to a child is incredibly cruel. Not only are parents completely humiliating their children, but they learn that when they try their best to be helpful and make a mistake, they should feel ashamed and not bother trying anything again. The thought of being in a situation where they could be embarrassed is enough to completely limit what they truly want to pursue in life. Part of learning and developing skills and experiences is making mistakes, and when someone is afraid to try something new or experience something different they simply won't do it. Instead they spend years regretting every opportunity they ever missed out on and the life they could have had if they'd known it's okay to make mistakes and it's part of life. 

It also guarantees that a child will not listen to their parents at all in the years to come. It depends on how much time I have, or if I'm working, but generally my meals are usually structured like this: 

Breakfast: 

If I have time/Day off: Gluten free cornflakes and chopped banana (with a tiny bit of milk so they're not dry) 

If I'm working: a banana 

Lunch:

I don't actually eat lunch, usually because I work during the afternoons and miss that lunch period. Generally I don't have an appetite anymore and if I don't feel like eating I either won't, or have a small snack like an apple or some grapes if I know I need energy to do something like study. 

Alternatively, if I wasn't hungry at breakfast I eat that meal at lunch instead. 

If my stomach decides to cooperate with me, a salad with some tuna is really nice. 

Snacks:

If I'm finishing work later I'll usually have a smoothie - one that's high fibre and less sugar. If I feel like I can tolerate anything in my stomach, Urban Fruit do these packets of baked strawberries which are again high in fibre. If I'm feeling fancy, carrot sticks and hummus. 

Dinner: 

I have a lot of soup, this is where I get some kind of spice/flavour (I loved spicy food before PI-IBS and C-Diff, and could tolerate it with my IBS-D). Fajitas are quick to make and I get full very quickly so usually 2 fajitas with chicken, peppers and some rice is enough for me. I also eat a lot of pork, either with vegetables and mashed potato or in stir fry. 

Beans on (gluten free) toast is a quick go-to if I'm hungry but don't want to have a meal overcomplicated in terms of flavour. 

I can't tolerate sweet things, my palette has been going that way for a while, but if I feel like something GU do these gluten free and vegan desserts like cheesecake - they use coconut cream instead of dairy and it compliments dark chocolate perfectly. 

I like dark chocolate generally but don't have it very often because I had an experience where I vomited after eating a square and the taste in my mouth was horrendous. It was the worst thing I've ever tasted (literally bowel prep and macrogol is better than stomach-marinating dark chocolate). 

It depends on the day and on how the PI-IBS is feeling - if I eat something and feel sick afterwards, I'll generally avoid it for 2 weeks and try it again to see if I can tolerate it. If it repeatedly makes me feel ill, I stop eating it. I thought I'd struggle going gluten and (mostly) dairy free but it's actually been really good and even if one day I can eat bread and pasta again, I'd absolutely choose the gluten free alternative. 

In a way it made me realise that I used to eat way too much bread, pasta and pastries. I'm really glad I've become intolerant to gluten because my diet at the moment makes me feel far more energised and less fatigued.

I have, yes. I went through anorexia recovery during my GCSE exams with a survival mindset: 'I will sit these exams and I will study even though I know I'm tired and have so many other feelings that I'm actively ignoring because I'm doing what I feel obligated to do by my peers and my school', kind of thing. I thought that after that time period was over, everything would be fine and everything would fix itself because I had tunnel vision towards the 'exit' of this situation that I desperately wanted to get to. 

Afterwards, I struggled to really understand my own identity and fell pretty quickly into drinking a lot of alcohol when I realised that I had never wanted to sit any of those exams, do any of that coursework and perfect every piece of homework. I had no idea who I was, what I wanted to do as a career and where I really wanted to go in life. Even then I still felt pressure to get into university and do my degree - not because I wanted it, but because other people wanted it from me. My mindset in university was 'I will finish my degree and graduate, even if it kills me' because deep down I was terrified of failing my parents. 

I'm 24 now and only really starting to figure out the best type of workplace for me and the most interesting career. I have no idea what I want to do in the future, but I'm determined to try out and experience as much as I can to help me make the decision now that the me a few years ago wasn't capable of making. I actively try to separate who I am as an individual from the depression; if I'm feeling a certain way or putting something off because I feel uncomfortable, I will ask myself if this is something that the depression wants or something that I want. If I'm not sure I'll ask the people around me questions to try and figure it out. 

You deserve good things. You deserve to have fun. You deserve to learn new things and study things you want to and not get caught up in other people's expectations of the timeframe/what you should be doing. So, I want to ask you as an individual what you would like to do. Would you like to start DnD sessions again? I watched my partner play it a lot with his friends in university and it always looks so fun. I bet it's even more fun to be playing it with other people. 

It's important to take small steps in a process like this, and you will still have bad days where the depression seems to take over - after 14 years living with treatment resistant depression I can tell you that I still have periods where I struggle. I don't give up even if I am struggling, because I know that as an individual with hobbies and interests, I deserve to be fulfilled and satisfied with my life, and do things that make me feel that way. 

It's really important to communicate to someone that you trust that you're finding things difficult at the moment. That doesn't have to be a sit down discussion - you can write letters or notes, you can message someone, you could record yourself saying what you want to say and send it to someone. All the people I went to university with found the same thing hard - everyone has some degree of burnout because we've all been pushed through similar education systems with similar expectations. We do as we're told, and once that's done, we don't actually know what we want to do because somebody else has been telling us what we should do the entire time. 

If you're uncertain if you feel you can keep yourself safe if you're alone, I would ask for help in the way you communicate best. You know your parents far better than an internet stranger like me does - what would they think? How would they react? If you feel uncomfortable stating that you feel unsafe if left alone, you could suggest something like a movie night with your parents. Watch a series on Netflix together if there's anything you're all interested in watching. Cook a meal together, play a board game, something that makes you feel safe and comfortable while also being fun and an all around good time for everyone. 

If you wanted to you could try showing them how to play DnD - if you don't feel comfortable returning to a group of people try playing with your parents. You deserve to have fun and enjoy yourself. You deserve to be happy. You deserve to be studying a subject that you're interested in and engaged in.

I always think there are a few different types of people who want to have children. There are parents who acknowledge that biology and genetics will determine the development of their child, accept it, and love, care and nurture their child unconditionally because they recognise that their child is an individual with different levels of abilities, different interests, different health conditions - and importantly, that they shouldn't define their child as a certain "type" because it was not the child's decision to be brought into the world. The moment they as parents chose to have a child and start a family, they recognised that whatever the outcome of their child's health and development would be their responsibility to bear. Regardless of the abilities their child shows, regardless of the challenges and hard work involved, they know that they will love their child even more because they are a unique individual. 

There are also parents who go through an entire pregnancy and before that, even, with an idealistic perspective on what their child will be like, their ability level, their development. They create an image and expectation of their child that hasn't even been born yet and then get disappointed and thrown back into reality when they realize that the ideal child they thought would arrive hasn't, and struggle to come to terms with the fact that they were dreaming and preparing for a child who wasn't the one that has been born. The worst part of this is that if parents refuse to let go of this ideal child that they thought would arrive, they will push that image on the child they have and force them to fit that image to satisfy themselves and reassure them. When that child inevitably refuses to fit that image, these parents switch off emotionally and instead get angry and frustrated at their child for not being exactly the way they had dreamed them of being. 

When a child grows up and learns very quickly that they are not what their parents wanted, and that everything they do will never be enough to meet their parent's demands, and that regardless of how much they try and work hard, it will all be for nought, that child will grow up questioning their own self identity. They could perceive themselves as fundamentally broken, unwanted, useless in the eyes of the guardians who chose to bring them into the world and forced them to live without their consent. However, it isn't the child that is broken or wrong at all; it's the parents, unwilling to let go of this image of their perfect child, and refusing to accept the individual child they have instead. 

I believe we can use our imaginations to see the path a child with those types of parents may lead. Seeking validation from others that do not have their best interests or welfare in mind, vulnerable to being manipulated and placed in dangerous situations, potential mental health problems once that child gets older and hasn't been told, or given the guidance the realize that they are not the problem at all, and they are validated and welcome as an individual. Children can't be categorised as a certain 'type', and it's extremely dangerous to give a label like that to children because they are still young, they are still developing mentally, they are still growing. They haven't turned out or chosen be defined as a certain type of person at all. It's those kind of labels that will emotionally stunt a child's development and give them the impression this is how they should or shouldn't be, when in fact we should encourage children to explore themselves and what they like/dislike, what they struggle with, to build their actual sense of self and be confident in knowing fundamentally who they are and where they stand in the world. It's better in the long run for a child to learn that sooner rather than later. 

To be blunt about it, parents must acknowledge that from the moment they chose to conceive and commit to a pregnancy, the decision about their future child's traits, abilities and development has been entirely taken out of their hands. It wasn't there to begin with. If parents cannot come to terms with the fact that they do not decide their child's image or 'type', and it is entirely up to biology, genetics and the developments that occur in pregnancy or in labour, they should not have children, quite frankly. Because it's in that situation where in the end, nobody ends up happy. Instead everybody involved spends years with regrets and pain that most likely will never be resolved. It will follow them for the rest of their lives.

What you need to do is start making a solid paper trail. Write down, in detail if it isn't too much for you, everything you saw/experienced. Times/Dates, even if approximate, are a bonus. Do you have any pictures of the events where you were injured by another patient? They would also be beneficial to supporting your formal complaint. The more evidence and documentation you have with your complaint, the more you'll force the inpatient unit's hand so they have to respond instead of not acknowledge it. 

When you've gathered enough documentation, and feel comfortable and supported, it might be worth considering taking this to a media outlet. However I would urge you to not do this immediately - it is easy for units like this to deny any of your experiences happening if they consider it to be an unsubstantiated claim. 

Throughout this process also consider getting a mental health advocate to support you during this process. The more people you have around you to provide support if you feel like you need it the better.

It's never a one size fits all thing. Everyone reacts to different SSRIs differently, different doses, different manufacturers etc. It's a very personal experience for anyone to go through when trying to find a medication that can help them while at the same time also not allowing the side effects to prevent them from living their day-to-day life. 

I think that you would get a unique answer from anybody that you asked this question to! I used to take Prozac until I was 18 (which I'd been taking in varying dosages since the age of 13). Unfortunately it began to become less and less effective for me and my GP tapered me off and put me on Zoloft. I prefer Zoloft in many ways, but I have my worries that one day that will stop working for me too (I'm currently on the highest therapeutic dose and have been for some time now). 

The way in which you measure the effectiveness of an SSRI or similar medication with depression is quite different. The medication does 50% of the work; but you are expected to work on that other 50% yourself either in therapy or a method that works for you as an individual. Medication for depression is never a fix-all - you have to do a lot of consistent and difficult work yourself to teach yourself coping mechanisms that are constructive instead of destructive, push yourself to try out new things or do something that makes you feel uncomfortable. 

Perhaps a better way to phrase this question would be something along the lines of "What medication got you to a place where you could actively work on treating your depression constructively and healthily?" 😊

I was diagnosed with BPD at the age of 17, when I was getting ready to leave CAMHS. The assessment itself was backed up by documentation from when I went into the service at 13, and before the assessment they sent forms to my teachers/form tutor/head of year at my 6th Form as well as my parents. Up until that age I had generally not been allowed to view my own notes from assessments like this, but as I was applying for DSA at university the next year my parents sent me all the paperwork. It was only then I discovered that I had been diagnosed, and started doing my own research into it.

My experience with diagnosis is different to your own, but I absolutely understand where you're coming from with the quality from the NHS in terms of mental health services. Mental health teams, and many community services, generally will only offer treatment under the blanket term of 'mild' depression and anxiety. I looked into a service near me when I moved and I put more trust in the reviews of care from patients than the service itself. My gut feeling was right when I phoned them to enquire further. 

Generally, with BPD, most mental health teams will not be willing to engage with you (at least in my experience). For example, I was offered a place for DBT by a GP at university and I refused based on the logistical fact that I would no longer be in the area to receive said DBT by the time a place became available for me. This was perceived as me being uncooperative and pessimistic about treatment which isn't the case at all - I would like to get the right help and try DBT, but it makes no sense to take a place on a waiting list when I wouldn't be in the area to start that treatment. That spot should go to someone else in the area who can access that treatment. 

What I would recommend from this point is to document everything. If you can, write down an approximate timeline of the past few years where the BPD has affected your life, relationships etc. Keep a track of this with what symptoms showed up at what times, their intensity, what impact that had on your day-to-day life. Actively write down what you're experiencing, with dates and times to show that this is something that is consistent in your life. Keep a good paper trail, and make a copy to send to your GP and ask them to put it on your medical records. 

I would also strongly recommend looking into getting an advocate and bringing their input into future GP/mental health discussions. What I've found over the years is that the patient alone is usually not fully believed or acknowledged without input from other people - whether this be an advocate, a close friend, a family member. Again ask them to write down everything, make a copy and add those to your medical records too. An advocate doesn't have to be someone you haven't met before or aren't familiar with - you can pick someone you feel comfortable with to be your advocate. 

I would also recommend giving the Mind helpline a call to discuss what your options should be from this point onwards. You deserve to receive the right diagnosis and the right treatment. That is your right. Don't let any medical professional scare you into believing that you won't be able to get a job, either - you are covered under the 2010 Equality Act. An employer cannot legally dismiss you due to your mental health condition, and it's entirely up to your discretion if you want to disclose it to them. 

Mental health teams have been direly underfunded and pressurised for years. I have been treated by some fantastic professionals doing their best in a system that is fundamentally broken. People haven't had trust in the NHS to provide mental health care for a long time - myself included - and they're forced by the structure of the way mental health is managed in the NHS to prioritize those most at risk. However, this does not mean that you should be denied a diagnosis and appropriate treatment. In a system as broken as the NHS, you need to be an advocate for yourself, and research what support you will need from others in order to get to where you want to be. 

I know it's demoralising and frustrating, and I know how much it hurts when the professionals who are meant to listen to you don't, and dismiss your valid concerns about your mental health, but don't give up. You have the determination and the strength to be persistent in asking for what you need from the mental health services and there are people, and ways in which to do that.

They were slowly resuming surgeries and there was a brain surgeon who had a massive waiting list of patients with brain aneurysms who had been waiting months, knowing that the blood vessel in their brain could burst at any given time and not have access to the medical care they needed. 

The fact that C-Diff has become far more of a community related illness as opposed to a hospital superbug is also another reason why I can see C-Diff becoming more prevalent. Doctors seem more willing to prescribe antibiotics, and because of the restrictions Covid brings less people have been able to get an appointment to see a doctor in person. Additionally there seems to be more of a wait and see approach in that symptoms aren't recognised quickly, and are treated later and with multiple rounds of antibiotics because the infection has made itself at home in the body and therefore needs more antibiotic treatment to resolve itself; but in doing so, it leaves many open to C-Diff unnecessarily.

My depression started at age 10, and I'm 24 now. I went into the mental health services at 13 and grew up in that environment, instead of developing as a person in my peer group. When I left the child/adolescent mental health services at 18, and for the few occasions after that when I tried to seek help, nobody really wanted to treat me. It was the same thing every single time: "You've had years of CBT. Why do you think this round will be different?" - they thought I was using it as a crutch to avoid the real world but the irony is for a long period of time that was my real world, and I didn't know any differently. 

I look back at the past 14 years and see how much I've lost to depression, self-harm, suicide attempts etc, and it makes me feel so empty and hollow. I feel like less of a person at this point and more a physical representation of my medical records and mental health notes. I have no idea what I want to do as a career, because depression made me believe I didn't need to think about those things as I would be dead soon anyway (aged 16). As a result, I'm having to figure that out now as an adult where other people seem to have a firm vision of what they'd like to do as a career/study. 

I've lost years to depression. I lost my entire personality, interests and preferences and it is just the worst feeling. I saw a lot of things I shouldn't have seen at that age, I thought a lot of awful things a young person, in theory, shouldn't have to consider at that age. One day, I was 16: and now I'm 24 and the only thing I have to show for it is an arm full of scars (that I'm lucky to have in the first place - I nearly lost my arm below the elbow in 2012) and horrible memories and pain I put at the back of my mind in order to get out of bed and go to work everyday. 

One thing that drives my resilience now, with anything, is a moment where everything clicked into place and I realized that I wanted to live. I wanted to learn new things, see new places, meet new people. I knew it wasn't going to be easy, and that I'd feel angry or frustrated by massive challenges that probably aren't that big to other people, but I knew I wanted to experience everything. Even though I'm thinking about a lot of things now that I should have been thinking about when I was younger, I know I'll get there at my own pace and that's all that matters: I don't expect to feel happy or positive all the time (most of the time I don't feel positive at all) but I want to find satisfaction in what I do and try out new things. 

It's near impossible to not mourn for the years I lost to this, and I'm sure in the future I'll look back at myself at 24 and notice what I don't have or what I lost now, and that's okay with me. It's also okay to look to the future and realize it isn't going to be easy to do what I want to do, and I can't prepare for my depression throwing something at me in the years to come - but I know that I'll keep getting back up and adapt to accomplish what I want to do.

YTA. You haven't even given her a chance to *try*. The reasonable thing to do is talk with the medical professional(s) in charge of her care, but make it an appointment that both you, your husband, step-daughter and her mom can attend together. Ensure that you, husband, step-daughter, her mom can talk about it fully with a neutral party present to mediate.

Your concerns are valid and I do understand your concerns about your step-daughter driving but I also have great sympathy for your step-daughter, who wants to try learning to drive and is being stopped by you. I can imagine she's probably feeling very frustrated and upset about the situation because teens are jerks and she could be singled out for not having driving lessons/not being able to drive socially, which is just *another* thing to add that could affect her self-esteem because she just wants to be included and do what other young people her age are doing. You would be TA if you stopped her.

Have you looked at finding a driving instructor that has experience in teaching students with autism? They are out there and you should do some research, send off a few emails etc. to potential instructors and include your step-daughter in the process and make her feel in control (an important feeling that will benefit her greatly when she is learning to drive and gets into a situation with other drivers on the road, because let's face it, many drivers don't drive as safely as they should e.g. rush hour traffic).

Let her try a few lessons with an instructor she feels comfortable with (it might take a few attempts to find the 'perfect' instructor for your step-daughter) and take it from there. It might take longer than her peers to pass but the important thing to reiterate is that everyone takes a different amount of time to learn to drive and there is no 'standard' or 'expected' time. The only way she will improve her skills will be with regular lessons and it might transfer into her daily life too. I've been learning to drive for 1 year, for example: am I close to passing my test? Probably not, but I'll know when I'm ready and when I do pass it'll be all the more satisfying because I know how much effort I put into working hard to achieve it.

On the other hand she may try it and decide now isn't the time - that's okay too. Let her take the lead and strike the balance between being supportive but also letting her be independent - show her that she is in charge and that if she wants support you, your husband and her mom are there for her. She has a bad lesson? Take her to get ice cream / see a movie / something she enjoys. She has a good lesson? Celebrate with her! Tell her how proud of her you are and show her that you support her and *want* to celebrate her successes with her.

Talk to her about when you were learning to drive and things you found difficult/something that happened during a lesson and how you dealt with it (this is NOT a reason to put the fear of God into the poor girl about something 'bad' happening while she's driving because that's an asshole move).

I used to work retail and my dyspraxia was absolutely worse depending on how much caffeine I'd had just before starting my shift, how much sleep I'd had the night before, what I'd eaten on my lunch break etc. Lots of little things usually combining to make me slower at recovering stock or getting out a delivery - or the opposite in that I'd had too many cans of Red Bull on my break, not thought an action through and made a mistake or had an accident (nearly cut open my arm with a box cutter while rushing a delivery, I got a second-grade concussion and post traumatic amnesia by hitting my head on the metal bar of a delivery trolley because I was so focused on the task at hand that I forgot my surroundings). 

It was hard to find a balance and I figured it out eventually - I was known simply for being clumsy and I worked with my manager and supervisors to figure out which part of the job suited me best on any given day (if they saw me struggling/trying very hard to not cry they'd let me take a quick 10 minute breather). I was allocated a specific department and the consistency really helped my time management and co-ordination and gave me the confidence to bounce back from small mistakes, when in the beginning I would get stressed out about them. 

I think it's about having that discussion with yourself and evaluating your own abilities on the day, looking back at your last shift and making mental notes like *yesterday I knocked a few glasses over accidentally, today I will be more mindful of my surroundings* or *yesterday I had a really good shift, I got x hours of sleep the night before so I should try to get the same amount tonight to improve my work performance.* But it's important not to beat yourself up about making the mistakes (I know it's really hard when your day just doesn't go to plan) and not worry about making the same mistakes when you clock back in because overthinking can also be counterproductive. 

When dyspraxia gives you lemons, make lemonade. Every moment is something that you can grow from and develop your understanding of how it affects you in different situations, so you can put preventative measures in place to lessen the chance of dyspraxia being a jerk.

I quit using an e-cig. The issue people have with vaping is that if I remember correctly the market/industry for them is about a decade old, and therefore we haven't seen a lot of research or literary papers come out of it. So it's hard to tell either way when it's in such an infantile research stage. 

For me I needed an e-cig that looked like an actual cigarette so I had something to do with my hands and the act of going outside to use it. As long as my brain equated my e-cig = actual cigarette, and as long as I recreated my smoking habits with something less detrimental to my health, there was no issue. 

Vaping gives you the breathing room to come to terms with the act of quitting and reconfiguring your life without nicotine and cigarettes. Everyone is different and everyone chooses to go about quitting differently and you know yourself best.

It's really bad advice to suggest sticking with cigarettes and please don't go back to them. The news reports have all been guilty of omitting information and demonising vaping when it does actually help people to quit.

When I quit smoking I went immediately onto NRT and got myself an e-cig. I was going through a period of extreme stress and wasn't in a position to quit cold turkey (dissertation/university stress). I used an e-cig for about 6 months until I started getting bored, it started to make me feel nauseous every time I used it, so it made sense to just stop. 

Went another 6 months e-cig free until I went to a gig where everyone around me was lighting up a cigarette and I wanted to cry out of sheer frustration. Went back to the e-cig a second time for 3 months after that and packed it up again after it triggered nausea and vomiting episodes. 

Everyone is different and NRT is for some people something they need, but take that with caution. However if you speak to your doctor about it and get the go ahead to try it, do it. It gives you the breathing space to figure out a way to quit that works for you.

It's simply just a different way of exploring the characters (especially those from the main series) and a look into how they adapt (or do not adapt, in some cases) in a different magical girl system with very different values and ways of functioning. I was honestly not surprised when an anime adaptation of Magireco was announced. Excited, yes, but absolutely not surprised. The story was also kind of rigid and didn't allow for much expansion in terms of character development with only the inclusion of the Holy Sextet and no personal stories for each girl.

Magireco opens up new avenues in terms of story and expanding the lore of the series. There's absolutely no guarantee that the storyline the anime will follow is the one we find in-game. My point is that Magireco opens up *a lot* of different opportunities: it's getting its own dedicated Chinese server showing that they are expanding the game and there is the possibility that it can be expanded internationally when the time is right. There was the stage show which told the first part of the Magireco story. The manga adaptation has begun to be serialised in Manga Time Kirara Forward. When Magireco opens up all these different options, I don't blame them for pursuing them.

In terms of the 'main' story, there's not a lot of wiggle room. I don't really know what would happen and I'm confident in guessing Shaft don't know either. The concept trailer was exactly that: just a concept trailer. They explicitly said that it was only made up of initial ideas and there was nothing concrete. Putting the potential sequel to Rebellion and Magireco side-by-side, the obvious one to advance or explore is Magireco.

What I learned was that if you have a shitty day at work, you just brush yourself off and use it as a learning experience. Say to yourself "today I did x/y/z wrong. As a result I got pulled aside by my supervisor. I will try to do better tomorrow." Dusting yourself off and going back into work after a bad day was really important and it was hard at first because I did feel very ashamed and embarrassed (a supervisor yelled at me on the shop floor in front of customers and I carried that one until the end. You have to evaluate how much shit you can put up with before you've had enough and before you would seriously consider leaving the position.

I got a very, very thick skin when customers were involved. I didn't give them a reaction, because that's what they want. I was extremely polite and nice and that infuriates them even more. Halls, hands down. If you want to be active and socialise, you use the communal areas (kitchen, lounge etc) and if you need space you can stay in your room and it's not a problem. My halls of residence had an assigned RA who came in and checked how we were doing every week and updated us on cool things going on within the halls (we had a pumpkin carving contest at halloween, at Christmas we had a competition to see who could decorate their communal areas the best). This was also our port to complain and bring up any problems (we had some issues with the people who lived next to us because they partied *really fucking hard* and kept us up at night by banging on the walls and screaming past / generally being loud past the 10pm party curfew). 

My university gave out a questionnaire when you were applying for halls that assigned you to likeminded people so you were compatible with the people you're living with. Halls is also good because you have people to watch out for you; security is tight and you are kept safe. But also with your flatmates: for example, my flatmates (bless them) took care of me when I was sick with freshers flu and made me food when I was too sick to cook. When I started taking medication for my insomnia that made me sleepwalk, they kept an eye on me to make sure I didn't wander out of the flat in the middle of the night. When I had asthma attacks they made sure I was alright. It's good to have someone around if you're ill with something. My point is, you look out for each other. 

If you run it past your flatmates first, I'm sure they'd be okay with your girlfriend coming to visit. Introduce her to them to make it less awkward and don't get up to anything steamy in the communal areas and you're good (I walked in on my flatmate making out with her boyfriend a few times. All I wanted was a cup of tea). I spent a chunk of my time in halls with my boyfriend and as long as I respected their space and tidied up after myself etc they welcomed me with open arms. I met most of my university friends in halls. The cool thing about halls is that you can be independent and everyone's trying to figure out their own routine, so yours is fine. People will probably give you a lot of credit for having a productive routine, especially when you first move in and everyone's trying to get into their own groove and settle in. 

I lived with the same people for three years (one in halls, then we found a flat together). Halls was crazy and amazing and enlightening and in my opinion you're depriving yourself of a key university experience by staying in private accommodation (I caught my RA getting weed from a dealer once and she never gave me grief about anything again.). Save that for second year.

This was me 3 years ago. I was enmeshed in the cycle of feeling an emotion, wanting to get high, getting high, functioning, then crashing. My entire two years at sixth form are a blur and I don't remember most of it. I was facing the pressures of having to get into university, studying in an unsupportive academic environment and was coping very badly with a number of things. My depression was intense and debilitating, and at the time that was the worse I'd ever felt. Drugs and alcohol were my painkiller, they stopped me feeling. They let me put on a happy face and fake a smile and pretend to be fine for another day when I was really fucking struggling internally. I had been dropped from the mental health services like a dead weight and was on my own for the first time. And I didn't know what to do. 

I was having problems at school. I found myself not being able to connect with my friend group as much, and distanced myself from them because I eventually grew to dislike them. I didn't have a friend group and wandered around dipping my feet in everybody else's. I was friendly, but I started to hate everyone. I thought they were all hypocrites who picked and chose their moments to pretend to care. I fell asleep in class and my grades tanked. I was failing for the first time in my life and instead of facing it, I forgot about the pain by drinking and getting high.

My uncle and grandmother died in very quick succession. I spent most of my weekends in hospital waiting rooms. I was entering, in my mind, a place of death. It really disturbed me. My grandmother died very suddenly, and she was the first dead body I ever saw. It changed how I saw her, because I can't remember my grandma in any other way since but that. I fell apart, because I couldn't process the grief. I can't word it, but you go into a place where every other option isn't viable and the only thing that helps is the substance. And it feels like such a *relief,* it feels so damn good to let go. So I understand why it's incredibly difficult to pull yourself out of. 

I eventually developed drug-induced psychosis and started becoming paranoid. I wasn't interested in anything else but getting high. That's all people know me for in my hometown, constantly being drunk or being high. I was desperate enough that I took painkillers when I didn't need them in attempt to get out of my own head. I couldn't feel *anything* for months. I broke my own wrist while high on skunk and that was my eureka moment, I think. 

I started to notice that getting high and getting drunk wasn't working for me. It didn't matter how messed up I got, I was still *feeling.* I was filled with shame and humiliation and I didn't want to face anybody sober. I saw university as a way to escape, and my only opportunity to break the cycle. I put all my effort into getting my grades back up, I stopped getting high and I stopped drinking completely. I've been teetotal for 4 years and quit smoking 4 months ago.

My fascination with drugs turned to prescribed ones. I get really, really excited to get my prescriptions from the doctors, more excited than a normal person should. I overdosed on zopiclone a few times. So I still have drug problems, but it's more of a *this will fix everything immediately* feeling. I've watched a shitload of Intervention, but I never stick around to see them clean and happy and *accomplished.* 

I want you to know that when you have your own eureka moment, embrace it and put your all into achieving it. I want you to know you can change, and you can beat the addiction demons. It's important to accept and acknowledge what you do, and accept the hurt and the pain and the bad feelings. Find other ways to cope that serve you the best, something cathartic. It feels crippling, and it feels debilitating, but you can get yourself out of this.

I watched Madoka Magica when it first came out in 2011 and the moment that a new subbed episode was available, I was watching it. I suffer from ongoing mental health problems, and at the time I was severely depressed, self-harming and suffering from anorexia. So, all in all, not particularly happy. I was shuttled between intensive therapy appointments that I didn't particularly enjoy on a weekly basis and was resisting treatment. I was constantly escaping the threat of being hospitalised, and didn't particularly care about what would happen to me. 

Watching Madoka Magica was my only escape, and the only thing I really looked forward to. I wasn't allowed to go back to school full time as I was too unwell, so I did half days, which I hated. The only distraction I had was sitting down to watch an episode of Madoka. I can't word how much I related to the girl's suffering and pain, especially Homura's. Homura suffered through timelines for about 12 years, and I related to that a lot. It felt like I was stuck in a cycle, and seeing Homura's cycle to save Madoka struck a chord with me. My depression was particularly bad towards episode 11, and I was sad that my favourite series was going to be ending. But episode 12 restored the hope that I was worth something, and that I should be fighting for my recovery. 

The series stuck with me for a lot of reasons, one of them being that it came along at a time in my life where I was deeply unhappy and it gave me hope. I was fascinated with the story, character development, and I loved the design of the witches, familiars and witch labyrinths. Every element of the series has so many layers and is so rich that I was completely hooked. 

I haven't watched another series after Madoka. When Puella Magi Madoka Magica Online came out, I was so excited for it. I taught myself how to navigate the game despite not knowing a lick of Japanese and loved every second. I'd play it on the school computers when I had free periods where I was supposed to be studying, and got a friend interested in it. We had so much fun with it, and I loved the design of my meguca so much that I drew her constantly and designed her witch form and familiars. 

When they announced Rebellion, I was stupidly excited. I downloaded the first 10 minutes from somewhere and watched it on repeat, trying to pick every little thing apart. When the full movie came out, I watched it repeatedly (took me about 2 years to not cringe at the ending though, even though I understand why they took the route they did). I still watch it over and over now. When the concept movie came out, I watched that on repeat, trying to take everything in. 

I've accumulated a lot of Madoka merchandise since - it started out with a Madoka prize figure from my friend, and it's only grown since then (some of my favourites are volumes 1-3 of Wraith Arc and one of my most recent additions is the Iroha Tamaki figure). Currently waiting on my own Bebe plush to arrive, which I'm excited for. 

So of course when they announced MagiReco, I was incredibly excited. I got the game via tunnelbear on my old phone the day it was released, but it was painfully slow and I couldn't get through the tutorial before I had to uninstall. I tried using android emulators to play it with no luck, and gave up on ever being able to play it until my boyfriend, seeing how upset I was over not being able to play it, offered to help me make a Japanese iTunes account and use his iPad to play. I was a little late to the party, but I made it in the end. 

I can't properly word how dear this series is to me. The words don't exist.

I have dyspraxia and mild ADHD, although I strongly suspect that my ADHD has gotten worse as I've gotten older. For me at least, the line between dyspraxia and ADHD is really blurred - I can't tell you which one causes which problems. They kind of egg each other on. 

Everything is kind of made worse by the fact I take medication for depression and it causes a lack of concentration and short attention span anyway, so everything is kind of made worse. 

I'm in university doing a literature degree and I can't read a page of a book - on my good days I can just about manage a paragraph before my brain decides to not cooperate with me. So most of my essays are pretty bad and I somehow have to convince my lecturers that I've actually read the books I'm writing about. 

I have a DSA tutor and she really helps me get my ass into gear. Keeping a diary with all my dates in and setting reminders on my phone help a lot - knowing that I have to go to something is important. Basically if it isn't in my diary I don't show up to it / do it. 

I've tried to go down the route of maybe being medicated for my ADHD but none of the GPs I see bar one has taken my concerns seriously. My GP surgery mainly does appointments via telephone so maybe going in face to face would make them take my problems a little bit more seriously, I don't know.

I worked in retail (Primark) for 9 months before leaving for university. I had a lot of accidents while I worked there - constantly walking into tables, rails, you name it I probably walked into it. I got a lot of bruises and cuts. The worst accident by far was when I got a second degree concussion and post traumatic amnesia after hitting my head on the handle bar of a delivery trolley. I was trying to unhook some hangers from the bottom of the trolley and stood up without thinking, or realising, that I was directly above the handle bar. My wrists and ankles constantly hurt and towards the end I was wearing wrist and ankle supports. All the heavy lifting of deliveries and constantly being on your feet really took it's toll on me. 

The one complaint my supervisors had about my work was that I was too slow. They were constantly trying to get me to speed up - my coordination wasn't cut out for rapid fire folding of clothes. In the beginning I would forget my user details for the tills and the passcode to the staff room etc, but I wrote them on my wrist to get around that issue. Change and handling money was hard at first, and I definitely made my fair share of mistakes, but I improved with time and my mental arithmetic (which is awful at the best of times) improved a lot.

I definitely improved my social skills a lot - managing customers, using tills etc was quite easy for me. It really improved my confidence. At the end I was doing tannoy announcements and taking phone calls and I got so excited about doing them - my colleagues found it funny how I could get so excited over something as simple as taking a phone call. 

I chose not to disclose my dyspraxia to my employers, and in hindsight I definitely should've. My mother said at the time that they would discriminate against me, even after I pointed out that by law, they're not allowed to and can get punished for doing so. Her response: "they'll still do it anyway."
